The user works on many concurrent projects on a Mac (and mobile) — software, writing, research, whatever else. Right now there's friction in:

That resolves fine (it found the directory, since it printed the record message rather than an error). Let me check `get_dependencies` and `config.json` content.
Now let's record it and proceed with the conversation.
This is a good, rich starting sketch. Before I go further into the mechanics of stakeholders and requirements, I want to press on a few things about the problem itself — because you jumped pretty quickly into solution detail (Spaces, hotkeys, GitHub repos), and I want to make sure I understand the underlying need before we get attached to that shape.

A few questions, in no particular order:

1. **What's actually costing you right now?** Is it time lost re-arranging windows/tabs every time you switch projects? Things falling through the cracks because notes end up in the wrong place or nowhere? Projects that quietly die because there's no repository of "what's active"? Or something else — what prompted you to want to build this *now*?

2. **Magic wand test:** if this already existed and worked perfectly, what would a normal day look like that's different from today? Walk me through it a little.

3. You described quite a specific mechanism — Spaces, a hotkey overlay, GitHub-backed directories. If I zoom out one level: is the real goal "reduce the friction/cost of juggling many concurrent projects," and the Space-switching/hotkey/repo structure is *one way* to get there? Or is there something more specific about *this* mechanism that matters to you beyond that goal (e.g., you specifically want GitHub for other reasons, or you've already tried other approaches and they failed)?

4. How many projects are we talking about, roughly, at a time — is this "3 active efforts" or "40 things in various states of dormancy"? That shapes a lot.

You’re right, I’m jumping far too quickly into solution design — my apologies, I had been ideating and getting too far into the weeds. Let me describe my situation.

I have a bunch of projects that I’m working on at any given moment. Right now, for example, I’ve got two different house deals I’m working on, I’m developing the clarity agent, I’ve got two different research problems (one in game theory and one in economics), I’ve got a course I’m developing, I have a book coming out soon, and I’ve got nascent ideas for a bunch of other projects that may happen in the future, including an ISO/IEC standards push related to the book, a small thing I’m doing on the side with some lawyers around NCII/CSAM law, and this idea for Portal.

I need a way to manage all of this stuff without going insane, and I would very much like to be able to do it both on my desktop machine and my mobile device. If this tool is useful, maybe I’ll make it useful for other people in the future too, because I have all sorts of ideas for a “team project management tool” written up in yet *another* project directory.

At any given moment, TL;DR is that I’ve got a bunch of projects running, a bunch of half-baked ideas or projects on the back burner, and a deep archive of them. 

When I sit down at my computer, I’d love to always have a quick dashboard of the projects and be able to jump in to any of them. When I “jump in” to a project, that should give me a screen that’s *just* the stuff in the project, and let me focus on it.

Two things I use heavily in my current setup (which I think would continue to make sense) are Spaces and custom keyboards — I’m an enthusiastic builder of those, and very much prefer specially mapped keys that let me jump between things quickly and easily.

Another pattern that I’ve noticed that seems robust is that git repos have been *really* useful ways for me to store things. More and more, my projects are centering around .md and .tex files, with your occasional .docx and .xlsx and .pdf and so on, and some things that live entirely within web services, like LucidChart images. The logic of being able to branch and merge, and the commit history, is really useful. “Commits” — the logical experience, not necessarily the specific implementation — could happen either explicitly (“done with this chunk of work, let’s mark that as a border”) or implicitly (“let’s take a break for the evening and checkpoint”) because it’s easy to rewind if needed. Branching (“let’s consider this fork of the project idea”) is always explicit but also very helpful.

This does imply a need for both 2-way diffs and 3-way merges of files, which is easy for things like .md and .tex and code, but obviously less so for PDFs and so on… but I could think of ways to be flexible with that. 

On a mobile device, my needs are more variable, and I could easily imagine wanting to be able to access this from an untrusted device via a web service as well.

I’ve got all sorts of other thoughts, but this is sort of a snapshot of where my thinking is starting from.

content:
That context is exactly what I needed — thank you for pulling back and giving me the situation rather than the design. Before I fold this into the problem statement, requirements, and stakeholder docs, I want to press on a few things, because the answers will shape everything downstream (and the existing draft in `goal/problem.md` was written before I knew the real scope — it says "software, writing, research, whatever else," which badly undersells what's actually going on: two house deals, two research threads, a course, a book, an ISO push, a legal side project, Clarity itself, and a deep archive behind all of it).

**1. Pressure-testing the goal itself.** You've described "Portal" pretty concretely already — dashboard, Spaces, hotkey capture, git-backed directories, mobile access. Before I treat that as the destination: if it already existed exactly as described, what would you actually be able to *do* that you can't today? I ask because there seem to be two candidate "why"s bundled together, and they'd pull the design in different directions:

   - **(a) Reduce the tax of context-switching** — get from "sitting down" to "in flow on project X" faster.
   - **(b) Prevent silent decay** — stop back-burner and archived projects from falling off your radar entirely (the ISO push and the legal side thing sound like exactly the kind of thing that could quietly die from neglect).

   Is it both, is one primary, or is there a sharper "actual problem" underneath both? What's the worst version of Portal that would still count as a real win for you?

**2. What's actually broken today.** You already have Spaces and custom keyboards, and you clearly like them. What's the specific pain that makes "just use Spaces + keyboards better" insufficient? (E.g., is it that Spaces don't persist a *list* of what's active vs. back-burner vs. archived? That there's no single place to see everything at a glance? That opening a project still means manually recreating window/app state each time?)

**3. Scope vs. the team-tool idea.** You mentioned a separate directory with ideas for a multi-user team project management tool, and floated that Portal might grow into that "if it's useful to other people." For now, should I treat Portal as strictly single-user/personal, and treat multi-tenancy/sharing as explicitly out of scope (just a noted future aspiration, not something the architecture needs to accommodate yet)? Or is there a real near-term reason to keep the door open architecturally?

**4. The untrusted-device mobile case.** When you say you might need this "from an untrusted device via a web service," what's the actual scenario — borrowed/public computer (implying: leave no residue, maybe read-only, ephemeral session) vs. your own phone's browser (implying: full access, just not the native app)? That distinction matters a lot for what the security/auth model has to guarantee.

**5. How hard is the diff/merge requirement, really?** You flagged that 2-way diff and 3-way merge are easy for .md/.tex/code but not for PDFs, .docx/.xlsx, or things that live entirely in web services like LucidChart. Is "solve versioning for non-text files" a hard requirement for v1, or is "git tracks binary file history, no real diff/merge, and you handle rare conflicts by hand" good enough for now?

Once I have these, I'll write up the problem statement, stakeholder list (I suspect it's mostly just you right now, but I want to check whether collaborators — co-authors, the lawyers, an editor — ever touch Portal itself vs. just the project content it manages), and requirements, and show you a summary to confirm before we move to scoping possible solutions.

Good questions.

1. Both of those are among the key goals. Another important one is being able to look at and edit and work on a project wherever I am, even if I don’t have my laptop with me, and even if we’re in a temporarily network-disconnected state (eg on a plane). 

2. Right now I need to manage the project-to-Space mapping quite manually, remember which files and URLs are relevant to the project, set up the lab notebook structure for each project, manage all the git commits and so on, and so on, all by hand. This is time that I’d rather spend working on my projects. In a perfect world, I’d just say “open this project!” and everything I need is right in front of me, I’m editing and thinking about the project itself, and hitting “save” (ie commit and push) and jumping to another thing. I’d also have that central dashboard view, which doesn’t exist at all right now. And if I were at a café and had a great thought that I wanted to jot down, I wouldn’t have to write it in a note in Google Keep and then hope to transfer it into the right place when I got home, or be frustrated that I can’t see my project files *at all* from there. 

3. I definitely want to focus on the single-user idea first. The multi-user idea is something for the future, but I think this idea will evolve enough times before I even start thinking about multi-user that that should be a separate problem.

4. I’m not sure — I think I need to think through the use cases in more detail.

5. Git tracking binary file history and I handle conflicts by hand is fine for now. Fancy future versions may include adding diff/merge capabilities for more file types going forward.

Good — that adds a real third goal (device/network independence) and clarifies the pain well. A couple of things before I write this up:

**On goal (1), the offline/no-laptop point** — I think this actually splits into two different requirements, and I want to check I'm reading it right:

- *Laptop + no network* (the plane case): this is close to "solved for free" if Portal's design doesn't require a network call to open/work on a project — a local git clone is inherently offline-capable. I'll capture this as a hard requirement: core project access and editing must not depend on connectivity when you're on your primary machine.
- *No laptop* (any device, own phone or borrowed): this is the harder, still-open case — same territory as question 4 below.

Does that split match what you meant, or did you also need full offline capability on a non-laptop device (e.g., editing on your phone with no signal)?

**On question 4 (untrusted device), since you said you need to think it through** — rather than block on that, let me seed it as a proper open question with a few candidate scenarios, and you can react to the framing now or refine it later:

- *Glance-and-jot*: borrowed computer or public terminal, want to see what's active and drop a quick note. Should be read-mostly and leave no residue.
- *Own-phone-browser*: not the native setup, but your own device — probably fine to allow fuller access, sandboxed to that session.
- *Real-work-from-borrowed-hardware*: need to actually edit a .tex file or review a contract from a machine that isn't yours. This is the highest-risk, highest-value case, and probably the one that most determines the security model.

I'll write this into `goal/open-questions.md` as an open question ("what does 'access from an untrusted device' actually need to guarantee?") with strategy "thinking," flagged for a dedicated pass before we lock architecture. Reasonable, or do you want to hash it out now instead?

**One I don't think you've answered yet: stakeholders.** My working assumption is that right now, *you* are the only person who directly touches Portal — the co-authors, lawyers, editor, etc. interact with the underlying project content (a shared doc, a repo) but never open Portal itself. Is that right, or does anyone else ever need to see or touch Portal directly (even read-only)?

And one scope-boundary I want to confirm rather than assume: Portal orchestrates and points at your existing tools (Gmail, Signal, calendar, LucidChart) rather than replacing any of them — it's the connective layer, not a new inbox or task tracker. Right?

Once I have those, I'll draft `problem.md`, `stakeholders.md`, `requirements.md`, and `open-questions.md` and show you the whole picture before we move on to solution shapes.

I think that as far as disconnected mode, like any software it should work correctly in that mode. In our case that can be really simple: as soon as you disconnect create a local branch. When you reconnect (and we need some debouncing on this) you see if you can merge this branch into its parent branch transparently, and do so if possible. If not, if a true 3WM is required, then you notify the user that you’re out of sync and will need to sync before remerging with that revision — and we use the same 3WM flow that we would use when merging a branch.

Agreed on the open question.

Agreed that I’m the only user for the moment. All of this multi-user stuff is for this next thing.

It is definitely a connective layer and not a new inbox, task tracker, or whatever.

input.content:
# Problem Statement

At any given moment there are many live threads: two house deals, the Clarity agent itself, two research problems (game theory, economics), a course, a book about to ship, an early-stage ISO/IEC standards push tied to the book, a side project with lawyers on NCII/CSAM law, this Portal idea, and a deep archive of things that used to be active. Some of these are in flight, some are deliberately on the back burner, and some are dormant enough that they're at real risk of being forgotten entirely.

Managing that portfolio is currently a manual, per-project chore layered on top of the actual work: remembering which macOS Space belongs to which project, which files and URLs matter, hand-rolling a lab-notebook structure, and running git commits by hand. None of that is the work — it's overhead paid every time attention shifts between projects, and it scales badly as the number of concurrent and back-burner projects grows. The overhead shows up in three distinct ways:

- **Context-switching cost.** Resuming a project means manually reconstructing its working state — the right Space, the right browser tabs, VSCode, and whatever else (Preview, Illustrator, Terminal, Clarity). There's no "open this project" action; every switch is rebuilt from memory.
- **Silent decay of back-burner and archived work.** Without a single view of everything that exists, low-priority projects (the ISO push, the legal side project) can drop out of sight for long enough to die by neglect, not by decision.
- **No location-and-connectivity-independent access.** Work only really happens at the desktop, with a laptop, with network. A thought at a café goes into Google Keep and has to be re-filed later, or is lost; a flight with no wifi means either bringing the wrong tools or losing the time entirely.

*Framing check:* the goal as stated ("build Portal") was pressure-tested against these three "why"s. All three survived as real, independent motivations rather than one goal wearing three descriptions — see Success Criteria below, which is organized around them directly.

## Why This Matters

The cost isn't hypothetical productivity loss — it's specific projects going dormant past the point of recovery (a legal collaboration, a standards push that depends on momentum) and time that should go to the work itself being spent on manual environment reconstruction instead. The user is also an active builder of Spaces- and custom-keyboard-based workflows and has already converged on git repositories as a durable, versioned storage substrate for project material — Portal's job is to remove the manual labor around that pattern, not to replace it.

## Scope

**In scope:**
- A personal, single-user tool for organizing, resuming, and checkpointing many concurrent/back-burner/archived projects.
- Git-backed project directories with a standard, auto-scaffolded substructure (active-file list, lab notebook, etc.).
- A home dashboard for seeing and jumping into any project.
- "Opening" a project: reconstructing its working environment (macOS Space, associated apps/files/URLs) without manual setup.
- A single checkpoint action that commits and pushes project state, available both as an explicit action and an implicit/automatic one (e.g., on session end).
- A frictionless, low-effort global capture mechanism (system-wide hotkey, "/command" entry) that files notes into a global lab notebook.
- Working with no network connectivity from the primary machine, with disconnected work reconciled automatically on reconnect where possible.
- At least some level of access from secondary/mobile/untrusted devices (the exact capability level is an open question — see `open-questions.md`).

**Out of scope (for now):**
- Multi-user or team support. A separate "team project management tool" idea already exists in its own project directory; Portal is deliberately being solved as a single-user problem first, and the two are treated as distinct problems rather than one general design.
- Replacing existing communication or task tools (Gmail, Signal, calendar). Portal is a connective/orchestration layer over these, not a new inbox or task tracker.
- Native diff/merge support for non-text file formats (PDF, Office docs, LucidChart, etc.). Git's binary version history plus manual, by-hand conflict resolution is sufficient for v1; richer diff/merge for these formats is a plausible future enhancement, not a current requirement.

## Success Criteria

Because this problem has three distinct "why"s, success is evaluated against each:

- **Context-switching cost:** "opening" a project is a single action that leaves the user actually looking at and working on the project's content — not arranging windows or hunting for files. "Checkpointing" out of a project is similarly a single action.
- **No silent decay:** the dashboard makes every project — active, back-burner, archived — visible at a glance, so a project only stays dormant because it was chosen to, not because it was forgotten.
- **Location/connectivity independence:** work continues seamlessly with no network on the primary machine, and a stray thought can be captured from wherever the user happens to be, landing in the right place without manual re-filing later (unlike the current Google Keep workaround).

The deeper signal of success is behavioral: the tool gets used daily instead of being abandoned the way ad hoc workarounds (like Keep-then-refile) have been.

# Stakeholders

## The user (sole direct stakeholder)

**Type:** aligned
**Engagement:** direct

**Characteristics:** Technically sophisticated builder; already runs a customized macOS environment (Spaces, custom keyboards) and uses git as a general-purpose storage/versioning substrate well beyond code. Comfortable with git branching/merging semantics as a mental model.

**Goals:** Reduce the manual overhead of managing many concurrent, back-burner, and archived projects; never let a project decay from neglect rather than choice; be able to see, resume, and capture into any project regardless of device or connectivity.

**Concerns:** Tooling that becomes its own maintenance burden or gets abandoned the way prior workarounds (e.g., Google Keep for stray notes) were — any friction in daily use is a real risk to adoption.

## Collaborators on underlying project content (indirect)

Co-authors, the book's editor, course collaborators, and the lawyers on the NCII/CSAM side project. These people never interact with Portal itself — they interact with the shared artifacts (a manuscript, a repo, a document) that live inside a Portal-managed project directory.

**Type:** aligned
**Engagement:** indirect

**Goals:** N/A directly — their interest is in the integrity and availability of the shared work product, not in Portal as a tool.

**Concerns:** If Portal's versioning or automatic-merge behavior ever corrupted or silently lost content in a shared artifact, these are the people who would be hurt without ever having chosen to use Portal. This is why the reconciliation/auto-merge behavior (see `requirements.md`) must fail safe to manual resolution rather than guess when correctness is uncertain.

## Whoever holds a device used for untrusted/secondary access (potentially adversarial, indirect)

Anticipated but not yet fully characterized — resolving this depends on the open question about what "access from an untrusted device" actually needs to guarantee (see `open-questions.md`). If the answer involves borrowed or public hardware, then anyone with physical access to that hardware after the session becomes a potential adversarial stakeholder (residual credentials, cached content, browser history).

**Type:** adversarial (in this specific context only)
**Engagement:** indirect

**Goals:** Gain access to project content or credentials they're not entitled to, via a device the user no longer controls.

**Concerns:** N/A (adversarial).

## Future stakeholders explicitly out of scope

Other individual users, and any team/organization that might eventually use a multi-user descendant of this tool, are explicitly not stakeholders for this problem. That idea is being tracked as a separate project.

# Requirements

Any solution must:

## Functional Requirements

1. Provide a home dashboard showing all projects — active, back-burner, and archived — at a glance, from which any project can be opened.
2. Provide an "open project" action that reconstructs the project's working environment (the associated macOS Space, and the files/URLs/apps tied to that project) without manual setup.
3. Store each project as a git repository with a standard, auto-scaffolded substructure (e.g., an active-files list, a lab-notebook directory) applied consistently across projects.
4. Provide a single "checkpoint" action that commits and pushes the current project state — available both as an explicit action ("done with this chunk of work") and as an automatic/implicit one (e.g., end-of-session checkpointing).
5. Support explicit branching of a project (a deliberate fork of the idea), using standard git branch semantics, with a merge flow back into the parent when appropriate.
6. Provide a frictionless, system-wide capture mechanism (hotkey, "/command" entry) for notes and commands that lands in a global lab notebook, without requiring the user to first identify or open the relevant project.
7. Support disconnected work from the primary machine with automatic reconciliation on reconnect:
   - On disconnect, work continues locally (e.g., on an automatically created local branch).
   - On reconnect (debounced, so brief connectivity blips don't trigger premature sync), attempt to merge that local work back into its parent automatically.
   - If automatic merge isn't safe, notify the user that a real three-way merge is needed, using the same manual merge flow used for explicit branches — never silently guess.
8. Provide some level of access to the dashboard and project content from secondary/mobile/untrusted devices. The exact capability level (read-only glance vs. full edit; own device vs. borrowed hardware) is pending resolution of the open question in `open-questions.md` and should be treated as provisional until then.

## Non-Functional Requirements

### Performance
- Opening a project and reaching the dashboard should feel effectively instant — no perceptible manual setup step between "I want to work on X" and "I am working on X."

### Security
- Handling of untrusted/secondary-device access must not leave durable credentials or cached project content on hardware the user doesn't control. Specific guarantees are pending the open question in `open-questions.md`; this requirement will be sharpened once that's resolved.

### Reliability
- Version history and durability must be strictly better than the current manual per-project git setup: no scenario should lose work that manual git usage would have preserved.
- Automatic reconciliation (requirement 7) must fail safe: when it can't be certain a merge is correct, it must stop and hand off to the manual three-way-merge flow rather than silently produce a possibly-wrong merge. This matters especially for shared artifacts touched by collaborators (see `stakeholders.md`).

### Usability
- Capture-to-filed-note friction must be at or below the level of the current ad hoc workaround (jotting in Google Keep), or the tool will suffer the same fate — abandonment in favor of whatever is fastest in the moment.
- The tool must hold up under daily use as the actual entry point for switching between projects, not just an occasional dashboard glanced at.

## Constraints

- Primary platform is macOS, built around Spaces and system-wide custom hotkeys as the existing, preferred interaction pattern — not a pattern to be replaced.
- Storage substrate is git (project directories as repositories, most likely GitHub-hosted); this is an established, deliberate choice, not open for reconsideration in this pass.
- Single-user only for the foreseeable future. A separate multi-user "team project management tool" idea exists as its own project and is out of scope here (see `problem.md`).
- No native diff/merge UI is required for non-text formats (PDF, Office documents, LucidChart, etc.) in v1 — git's binary version history plus manual conflict resolution is sufficient; richer support for these formats is a future enhancement, not a current requirement.
- Must integrate with, not replace, the user's existing tools and workflows (Gmail, Signal, calendar, browser, VSCode, Illustrator, Preview, Terminal, Clarity, LucidChart, etc.).

# Open Questions

## Q1: What does "access from an untrusted/secondary device" actually need to guarantee?

**Status:** open
**Why it matters:** This determines the security model and the shape of mobile/web access (requirement 8 in `requirements.md`), which in turn affects architecture decisions (how much lives on-device vs. server-side, whether a hosted service is needed, what "sandboxed session" means). Getting this wrong either over-builds security for a case that doesn't happen, or under-builds it for a case that does.
**Strategy:** thinking
**Findings:** Three candidate scenarios were proposed as seeds for the discussion, not yet confirmed or prioritized:
  1. *Glance-and-jot* — borrowed/public computer, wants to see what's active and drop a quick note. Read-mostly, must leave no residue after the session.
  2. *Own-phone-browser* — user's own device, not the native setup, but a device they control. Probably safe to allow fuller access, sandboxed to that session.
  3. *Real-work-from-borrowed-hardware* — needs to actually edit real content (e.g., a .tex file, review a contract) from hardware that isn't theirs. Highest risk, highest value, and likely the case that most determines the security model.

# Solution

## Chosen Approach

Portal is a native macOS app that directly owns the core verb: "jump to a project and have everything ready." It doesn't delegate Space-switching or app-launching to existing window-manager tooling — the user has no existing setup worth building on (a manually-maintained, unreliable mapping of Spaces to cmd+option+digit hotkeys), and owning this directly is what makes it possible to *infer the current project from the current Space*, which the capture flow depends on. A lightweight, separate mobile client provides full view/capture/edit access from the user's own phone, talking directly to the same git-backed data rather than mirroring the Mac app's job (there's no "Space" concept on a phone, so it doesn't need to).

### Key design decisions

**1. The Mac app owns Space assignment and inference, end to end.** Opening a project means: find the Space already assigned to it (or find a free one, or create a new one if none is free), switch to it, and launch/arrange the associated files, URLs, and apps per that project's manifest. The reverse also holds: at any moment, the app knows which Space is active and can map that back to "which project is this," which is what makes context-aware capture possible.

**2. Space↔project mapping is local, machine-specific UX state — it does not sync.** It lives in the Mac app's local storage, not in any git repo. A Space number on this Mac means nothing on another Mac or on a phone, so syncing it would be actively wrong, not just unnecessary. This is a hard boundary: anything that's "this machine's session arrangement" stays local; anything that's "the actual state of the project" goes in git.

**3. A central "Portal home" repo holds cross-project metadata.** This repo — not any individual project — is the source of truth for the project registry (every project's name, state: active/back-burner/archived/pinned, and location) and hosts the root/global lab notebook that captures land in in when there's no current project context. It plays the same role for Portal-as-a-whole that each project repo plays for itself.

**4. The lab notebook / TODO list / file-and-URL collection is one reusable template, applied twice.** The same standard substructure the user already wants inside every project repo also describes the Portal home repo's own notebook. Building it once as a shared pattern (rather than a special-cased root version) keeps the two consistent and halves the design work.

**5. Capture is context-aware.** The global hotkey opens a quick-entry console. If the current Space maps to a project, the note is appended straight into that project's lab notebook; if not, it goes to the home repo's global notebook for later filing. This removes the "where does this go" decision at the exact moment friction is most costly.

**6. Implicit checkpoints are commits too, just tagged differently.** Rather than treating "explicit commit" and "auto-save" as different mechanisms, both are git commits — auto-checkpoints just carry a distinct, machine-generated marker (e.g., a fixed prefix or trailer) that separates them from human-titled commits in the log. This gives a clean narrative view (real commits only) and full rewind granularity (every intermediate state) from the same history, with no separate storage mechanism needed.

**7. The disconnect/reconnect mechanism and the idle-based auto-checkpoint are the same primitive.** Both are "the system decided to checkpoint without being asked" — disconnection just adds "on a branch, to be merged back later" on top of the same tagged-auto-commit idea. One implicit-checkpoint mechanism, two triggers (idle timeout, connectivity loss), keeps this from becoming two parallel systems to maintain and reason about.

**8. The mobile client is a separate, lighter-weight thing, not a port of the Mac app.** Its job is dashboard (project list/state), context-free capture (there's no "current Space" to infer from, so it defaults to the global notebook or lets the user pick), and file view/edit — all against the same git-backed repos. It does not need to know anything about Spaces, window arrangement, or app-launching. Whether it's a native iOS app or a mobile-optimized web view is an implementation choice for architecture design, not a solution-shape decision — either way it's reading and writing the same repos, most likely via the git host's API rather than requiring the Mac app to be running.

## Alternatives Considered

**Orchestrate existing window-manager tooling (Hammerspoon/yabai/skhd) instead of owning Space logic directly.** Set aside once it became clear the user doesn't have existing tooling worth preserving — the current setup is a manually-maintained, already-unreliable mapping. More importantly, "infer current project from current Space" needs tight, first-class integration with Space state; bolting that onto a third-party tool's event model would be more awkward than owning it directly.

**Fully cloud-native product**, with a real backend/database as the primary source of truth and git as a mirror. Set aside: it inverts the established preference for git as the durable source of truth, and it's substantially more infrastructure (hosting, uptime, a real backend) than a single-user tool needs. This is the shape to reconsider only if/when the multi-user idea becomes real — a separate project, per `problem.md`.

## Open Questions, Risks, and Concerns

- **Feasibility of Space automation (tracked as `goal/open-questions.md` Q2, strategy: prototyping).** macOS has no public API for enumerating, creating, or switching Spaces programmatically — every tool that does this today relies on private/accessibility-layer behavior. This is now the single biggest technical risk to the chosen approach and should be spiked early in architecture design, before the rest of the app is built assuming it works. If it turns out to be infeasible or too fragile, the "Mac app owns Space logic directly" decision (design decision 1) would need to be revisited.
- **Untrusted/non-owned-device access (tracked as `goal/open-questions.md` Q1)** is now specifically relevant to the mobile client's architecture — whatever shape that client takes, its trust boundary needs to be designed with Q1's eventual answer in mind, not bolted on after the fact.
- **Debounce tuning for idle-based auto-checkpoints** is a real UX judgment call (too short → noisy history even with tagging; too long → a crash or force-quit could lose more than expected) — worth settling with actual usage data rather than guessing upfront.
- **Unified implicit-checkpoint state machine.** Because idle-timeout and disconnect are two triggers for the same underlying mechanism (design decision 7), they need to be designed as one state machine from the start — e.g., what happens if a disconnect occurs mid-idle-timeout, or the reverse. Flagging this now so it doesn't get built as two overlapping, subtly inconsistent systems. Worth a specific look during failure analysis.
- **Shared template spec.** The lab notebook / TODO / file-and-URL-collection pattern (design decision 4) needs an actual lightweight format spec of its own before it can be scaffolded consistently into both the home repo and every project repo — a natural early task in architecture design.

# Solution Summary

## What we're building

A native macOS app, Portal, that owns one core action — "open this project" — end to end: find or create the right Space, switch to it, and launch/arrange whatever files, URLs, and apps that project needs. Every project is a git repository with a standard internal structure (a lab notebook, a TODO list, a collection of relevant files/URLs). A separate "Portal home" repo holds the project registry (what exists, and whether it's active, back-burner, archived, or pinned) and a root lab notebook for anything captured outside a specific project. A lightweight mobile client gives full view/capture/edit access from your own phone, talking to the same repos.

## What it feels like to use

You sit down, glance at Portal's dashboard, and see everything — not just what's active, but what's waiting and what's archived, so nothing quietly falls off the radar. You pick a project (or hit a hotkey mapped to it) and Portal jumps you to its Space, with the right files already open in the right apps — no reconstructing anything from memory. You work. When you're done, one action checkpoints it: commit, push, done, and you jump to the next thing.

While you're in a project's Space, a system-wide hotkey pops a small console for a quick note — it lands directly in *that* project's lab notebook, because Portal already knows which project the current Space belongs to. Away from any project (or away from your desk entirely, phone in hand at a café), the same kind of note lands in the global notebook instead, to be filed later. Either way, nothing gets stuck in a notes app you'll forget to revisit.

If you're on a plane with no wifi, work just continues — Portal quietly checkpoints your changes locally, and reconciles automatically the moment you're back online. If that reconciliation isn't safe to do silently, it tells you and walks you through the same merge flow you'd use for a deliberate branch — never a silent guess.

Under the hood, most "saves" you never explicitly asked for — an idle pause, a dropped connection — still become real git commits, just tagged as auto-checkpoints. Your `git log` reads cleanly (your real, titled commits tell the story) while every intermediate state is still there to rewind into if you ever need it.

## How it addresses the problem

- **Context-switching cost** → the "open project" action replaces manual Space/file/app reconstruction entirely.
- **Silent decay of back-burner/archived projects** → the dashboard's project registry is the one place everything is visible, regardless of state.
- **Location/connectivity independence** → offline work on the primary machine is a first-class case (not a degraded one), and the phone gets full, real access — not a stripped-down companion view.

## Nonobvious design choices worth flagging

- **Portal owns Space logic directly rather than scripting an existing window manager.** The user had no existing tooling worth preserving, and inferring "current project" from "current Space" needs tight integration that a third-party tool's event model would make awkward.
- **Space↔project mapping never syncs.** It's local, per-machine UX state; only the project's actual content and the registry of what projects exist are shared via git. Syncing Space numbers across machines would be meaningless.
- **Idle-timeout auto-checkpoints and disconnect-triggered auto-branching are the same mechanism with two triggers**, not two separate systems — both are "implicit checkpoint," tagged distinctly from explicit commits.
- **The mobile client is deliberately not a port of the Mac app.** It has no Spaces to manage, so its job (dashboard, context-free capture, file edit) is much smaller, and it talks to the git layer directly rather than through the Mac app.

## Key open risk

There is no public macOS API for enumerating, creating, or switching Spaces — this is the single biggest feasibility question behind the whole approach, and it's flagged for an early prototyping spike in architecture design (see `goal/open-questions.md`, Q2) before the rest of the app is built on top of that assumption.

# Portal

Right now there's a graveyard problem hiding in plain sight: a pile of real, valuable projects — two house deals, two research threads, a course, a book about to launch, an ISO standards push, a legal side project, plus Portal itself — competing for one person's attention, with the connective tissue between them (which Space, which files, which git commit) all held together by hand. Nothing is actually lost, but the overhead of remembering and rebuilding context every time you switch is a real tax, and the projects that don't get attention can quietly die of neglect rather than by choice.

Portal is a Mac app that owns one job completely: jumping you into a project. Say which one, and it finds or creates the right Space, switches to it, and opens exactly the files, URLs, and apps that project needs — no manual reconstruction, ever. It knows which project you're in at any given moment, so a quick note dropped through a global hotkey lands directly in that project's own notebook, not a stray notes app you'll forget to revisit. Every project lives as a git repo with a consistent internal structure, checkpointing is a single action, and a home dashboard shows everything — active, back-burner, archived — so nothing dies quietly just because it wasn't looked at this week. It works just as well with no wifi on a plane, reconciling automatically the moment you're back online, and your own phone gets full, real access to the same projects, not a watered-down companion view.

It starts as a tool built for one very busy person to stop paying the context-switching tax — but the bones of it are general enough that it's easy to imagine it growing into something other people use too, someday, once it's proven itself here first.

**7. It applies equally to branching: an explicit `/branch` and an automatic disconnect-triggered branch are the same git-branch operation underneath, just triggered differently. And it applies to merging: reconciling a disconnect-branch back into its parent and merging an explicit, deliberate branch both go through the identical diff/3-way-merge flow — there is no separate "sync my offline work" mechanism distinct from "merge a branch." It talks to the git layer directly — most likely via the git host's API — rather than requiring the Mac app to be running.

That vocabulary — not the console itself — is the real interface to Portal's core actions. On Android, where a global hotkey and a typed console don't fit the platform's conventions, the same underlying verbs are exposed through touch-native affordances instead (e.g., a quick-actions sheet or share-target) — same grammar, different input surface per platform.

Portal file types split into "native" and "delegated."** The lab notebook, TODO list, and file/URL collection (decision 4) are examples of a more general concept: some file types are native to Portal, meaning Portal renders and edits them directly on every platform it supports, while everything else is a delegated file — Portal tracks a reference to it and hands off opening it to whatever app already handles it (Illustrator, Preview, a browser, Word). ## Q3: Does `gitoxide` (`gix`) have enough coverage for Portal's needs, or is `libgit2` (`git2`) required?

**Status:** open
**Why it matters:** The Rust core (see `solution/architecture.md`) needs to perform commit, branch, and — critically — three-way-merge operations identically on both platforms. `gix` is pure Rust (no C cross-compile step, uses `rustls` instead of juggling TLS backends per platform) and is what Cargo itself increasingly uses internally, which is a real maturity signal — but its porcelain-level coverage, especially of merge, was thinner than `libgit2`'s as of the source conversation. `libgit2`/`git2` is the more complete, battle-tested option but brings C toolchain and cross-compilation overhead for Android.
**Strategy:** prototyping
**Findings:** Not yet investigated. Should be spiked alongside Q2, early in architecture design — specifically, confirm `gix` can do a real three-way merge with conflict detection before committing to it; fall back to `git2` if not.

# Architecture

## Nouns and Verbs

**Project** — a git repository with the standard internal structure (lab notebook, TODO list, file/URL collection) plus a registry entry recording its state (active, back-burner, archived, pinned). One special Project, "Home," additionally holds the cross-project registry itself and serves as the root lab notebook for captures with no current-project context. Home is a Project, not a separate kind of thing — same structure, same operations, one reserved role.

**Space** (macOS-only) — a macOS Space, related to a Project through a mapping that exists only on the local machine. This is not a Portal-level noun in the shared sense; it's Mac-shell-local state.

**Checkpoint** — a git commit against a Project, either explicit (user-titled, via `/commit`) or implicit (idle-timeout or disconnect-triggered, machine-tagged). Same underlying operation, distinguished by tag, not by mechanism.

**Branch** — a git branch on a Project, either explicit (user-created, via `/branch`, a deliberate fork) or implicit (auto-created on disconnect). Same underlying operation as Checkpoint's split: one primitive, two triggers.

**Merge** — reconciling a Branch back into its parent, via the same diff/three-way-merge flow regardless of whether the branch was explicit or a disconnect-branch being reconciled on reconnect.

**Command** — a parsed instruction from the console (Mac) or quick-actions surface (Android): `/new`, `/open`, `/close`, `/commit`, `/branch`, `/merge`, `/note`, extensible. This is the verb layer of the whole system — everything a user does to Portal is one of these, invoked through a platform-appropriate surface.

**Note** — captured text that becomes lab-notebook content, filed into the current Project's notebook if one is inferable, or Home's notebook otherwise.

**File type** — a classification each file in a Project carries: *native* (Portal renders/edits it directly — the lab notebook, TODO list, file/URL collection today) or *delegated* (Portal tracks a reference and hands off opening it to whatever app already handles it).

## Major Components

### Rust core (shared library)

Owns everything that must behave identically on macOS and Android, and nothing that's inherently platform-specific:

- Git operations (commit, branch, merge/3-way-merge, push/pull, diff) against local clones.
- GitHub API client and auth (OAuth device flow).
- The implicit-checkpoint state machine (design decision 7 in `solution.md`): idle-timeout detection, disconnect/reconnect detection and debouncing, auto-branch-and-reconcile logic, all as one component with multiple triggers rather than duplicated per platform.
- Command grammar: parsing a Command string into a structured action and executing it against the local Project data.
- Native file-type parsing and manipulation (lab notebook, TODO list, file/URL collection) — the logic, not the rendering.
- Project registry read/write against the Home repo.

Exposed to both native shells through UniFFI-generated bindings (real Swift and Kotlin APIs, not hand-written JNI/C shims). Credentials are never persisted by the core — it accepts them via an injected callback, with each native shell backing that callback by its own platform's secure storage (Keychain on macOS, Keystore on Android).

### macOS shell (Swift/SwiftUI)

- Dashboard and console UI, calling into the Rust core for all data, git, and command operations.
- Space control: detecting the current Space, enumerating Spaces, creating/switching Spaces, via SkyLight/CGS private framework symbols (declared in a bridging header or resolved via `dlsym`) — see Q2. This is genuinely Mac-only and privileged; it doesn't belong in the shared core.
- App/file/URL launching for a Project's manifest, via `NSWorkspace`.
- Local, unsynced Space↔Project mapping storage (a local plist or SQLite file — explicitly not part of the Rust core's data model, per design decision 2 in `solution.md`).
- Keychain-backed credential storage.

### Android shell (Kotlin/Jetpack Compose)

- Dashboard and quick-actions UI, calling into the Rust core via its Kotlin bindings.
- Local git clones live in `context.filesDir` (real POSIX/ext4 semantics: symlinks, mode bits, case sensitivity, inotify) — not shared/external storage, which is FUSE-emulated and silently breaks git's executable-bit and symlink tracking. This is a hard constraint, not a preference.
- Long-running git operations (clone, fetch, large merges) run under `WorkManager` or a foreground service, because Android's background execution limits can kill an in-flight operation — the Rust core's operations need to be interruptible and resumable, not just "call and block."
- `.git` is excluded from Android auto-backup (`dataExtractionRules`) — a partially restored `.git` directory is silent corruption waiting to happen.
- Keystore-backed credential storage.
- A `DocumentsProvider` implementation is a plausible v1.1 addition (makes repo contents browsable from the system file picker and other apps) but isn't required for the core experience — deferred, not designed in detail yet.

### GitHub (external)

The actual durable storage substrate: one repo per Project, plus the Home repo. Both native shells and the Rust core treat it as the source of truth; local clones are working copies, not the canonical store.

## Key Technology Decisions

- **Rust core + UniFFI + native Swift/Kotlin shells**, rejecting Kotlin Multiplatform (its Kotlin/Native side has no mature git library — the one genuinely hard shared component, git, would fragment anyway) and rejecting a "shared spec, independent implementations" approach (real drift risk between two from-scratch implementations of the same behavior). This resolves the cross-platform strategy question flagged during solution brainstorming.
- **Git library choice (`git2`/libgit2 vs. `gix`/gitoxide) is not yet made** — tracked as `goal/open-questions.md` Q3, a prototyping spike alongside Q2.
- **macOS Space control via private SkyLight/CGS symbols**, not AppleScript (AppleScript can only blindly simulate the Mission Control keyboard shortcut; it can't detect, enumerate, or create Spaces, all of which the design requires) — tracked as Q2, revised from the earlier, overly optimistic "try AppleScript first" note.
- **Android git working trees live in app-private `filesDir`**, never shared/external storage — this is a correctness constraint (FUSE-emulated storage breaks symlinks and mode bits, which git depends on), not just a permissions convenience.
- **No Mac App Store distribution.** Using private frameworks forecloses App Store submission; the app will be signed/notarized and distributed outside the store. Flagging explicitly for confirmation — it's a real, sticky choice, not a detail.

## Cross-Cutting Concerns

**Security.** Credentials live only in platform-native secure storage (Keychain/Keystore), injected into the Rust core rather than persisted by it. Space↔Project mapping (local, unsynced machine state) never leaves the Mac. The mobile-access trust boundary for hardware the user doesn't own (Q1) is still unresolved and out of scope for this pass — the Android app built here is for the user's own device, which is already a settled, trusted case.

**Reliability.** The implicit-checkpoint/branch/merge state machine lives once, in the shared core, rather than being reasoned about twice — this is the main defense against the two platforms silently drifting in how they handle "the system decided to checkpoint without being asked." On Android specifically, git operations must tolerate being interrupted mid-flight (background execution limits) and resume cleanly rather than leaving a working tree in a half-finished state.

**Operations.** This is a single-user, no-backend system — there is no server to deploy, monitor, or page anyone about. "Operating" it means: crash logs stay local to each device, and the only external dependency with its own uptime is GitHub itself, which is already treated as a known, accepted single point of failure (noted during solution brainstorming, worth a line in failure analysis).

## Risks and Open Questions

- **Q2 (Space automation feasibility, revised)** — primary path is SkyLight/CGS private symbols; needs an early spike before the rest of the Mac shell is built assuming it works.
- **Q3 (git2 vs. gix, new)** — specifically needs validation that the chosen library supports real 3-way merge with conflict detection; this is load-bearing for the Merge noun across both explicit and disconnect-branch flows.
- **App Store distribution is being given up** as a consequence of the SkyLight approach — flagged for explicit user confirmation, since it's expensive to reverse once the app is built around private APIs.
- **`DocumentsProvider` and broader Android file-sharing** are deferred past v1 — noted so it doesn't get silently forgotten, not because it's unimportant.
- **CitC (client-in-the-cloud) is a plausible future direction**, not a current one — if Android's background-execution constraints prove too painful in practice, or if the multi-user idea ever becomes real, moving the working copy server-side is the natural next architecture. Not designed now; noted so it's not a surprise later.

# Threat Model Summary

Portal is a single-user, no-backend system — the threat surface is small by construction, but not zero. Top risks, ranked:

1. **Unsafe auto-merge corrupting shared content (high).** The implicit-checkpoint/auto-merge mechanism reconciles disconnected work automatically when it judges that safe. If it judges wrong, it could silently corrupt a project a collaborator (co-author, editor, the lawyers on the NCII side project) depends on, without them ever knowing Portal exists. *Mitigation:* fail safe by design — any uncertainty routes to the same manual three-way-merge flow used for explicit branches, never a silent guess.

2. **Space-control fragility (medium).** macOS Space detection/enumeration/creation relies on undocumented SkyLight/CGS private framework symbols — no stability guarantee across OS updates, and it forecloses Mac App Store distribution. *Mitigation:* prototype early (Q2 in `goal/open-questions.md`) before building the rest of the Mac shell on top of the assumption that it works; isolate the private-API calls behind a narrow interface so a future replacement is contained to one component.

3. **Git library coverage gap (medium).** `gitoxide` may not fully support 3-way merge with conflict detection, which the Merge operation depends on for both explicit branches and disconnect-branch reconciliation. *Mitigation:* validate via spike (Q3) before committing; fall back to `libgit2` if needed.

4. **GitHub as a single point of failure (medium).** Cross-device sync, mobile access, and eventually the untrusted-device access model (Q1) all depend on GitHub's availability and the user's account access to it. *Mitigation:* accepted as a reasonable dependency for a single-user tool — local clones on both devices mean work continues through transient outages and reconciles later, so it's a sync delay, not a hard stop.

5. **Android background-execution kill (medium).** Long git operations (clone, fetch, large merge) can be killed mid-flight by Android's background execution limits, risking an inconsistent working tree. *Mitigation:* run under WorkManager/a foreground service; design core git operations to be interruptible and resumable rather than atomic all-or-nothing calls.

## Single points of failure

- **GitHub account access** — losing access (compromised credentials, GitHub outage, account issue) blocks sync across every device at once. No alternative host is planned for v1; accepted risk for a single-user tool, worth a line in disaster-recovery thinking (e.g., can local clones alone reconstruct everything if GitHub access is lost?).
- **The Rust core's merge logic** — both platforms depend on the same shared implementation for a correctness-critical operation. A bug here affects both clients identically, which is the intended benefit (no drift) but also means there's no independent implementation to catch a shared mistake.

## Deliberately out of scope for this pass

- Threats specific to access from hardware the user doesn't own — blocked on Q1, which hasn't been resolved yet. This threat model covers the user's own Mac and Android device only.
- Multi-user/team threats (a different user's data, cross-tenant access) — out of scope per `problem.md`; this is a single-user system.

Real question, and worth digging into properly rather than waving it off. Let me break "Space handling" into its three actual sub-problems, because they don't have the same answer.

**1. Switching to a known Space — genuinely solvable with public APIs.** macOS has real, documented "Switch to Desktop N" keyboard shortcuts (System Settings → Keyboard → Shortcuts → Mission Control). Posting those keystrokes is a fully public, documented mechanism — `CGEventPost` (Core Graphics Event Services) can synthesize them directly from Swift; you don't even need to shell out to `osascript`/AppleScript, which is slower and less clean anyway. Caveat: it's index-based (Space 3, not "the Clarity space"), so if you ever manually reorder Spaces outside Portal, the mapping can drift — Portal would need to periodically re-verify, not just trust its own memory forever.

**2. Detecting the current Space — no public Space-ID API exists, but we may not need one.** There's no documented way to ask "what space number am I on." But `CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` *is* fully public and documented, and it returns which windows are currently on-screen. Since Portal already knows which windows it launched for which project, it can cross-check "are any of Project X's windows currently visible?" — a real, observed signal rather than an assumed one. Combine that with Portal's own record of "the last thing I switched you to," and you get a decent-confidence guess without ever touching Spaces internals directly. The nice part: this fails safe into behavior we already designed — when it's ambiguous, capture just falls back to the global notebook, exactly like the "no project context" case already does. We don't need certainty, we need a good guess with a safe fallback, and this gets there.

**3. Creating a new Space — this is the genuinely hard one.** There's no headless way to create a desktop; the only affordance is the "+" button inside the Mission Control overview itself. But here's the useful fact: Mission Control has real VoiceOver support, which means Apple exposes *some* Accessibility-API structure for it — the same public `AXUIElement`/System Events framework VoiceOver itself runs on, not a private framework. So the candidate approach is: trigger Mission Control via the public shortcut, walk its accessibility tree to find the "+" element, activate it, close Mission Control. That's automating a real, visible UI action through Apple's documented accessibility surface — a fundamentally different (and IMO much more defensible) risk than calling `CGSGetActiveSpace` via `dlsym`. It's undocumented *structure*, not an undocumented *API*. I can't tell you with certainty it'll work reliably without actually inspecting that tree — that's a real unknown, checkable in an afternoon with Xcode's Accessibility Inspector, not something I should assert confidently from memory.

One honest caveat: even fully avoiding private frameworks probably doesn't reopen Mac App Store distribution on its own — sandboxed App Store apps face separate restrictions on driving other processes via Accessibility/Apple Events (Apple rarely grants the entitlement for it). So this is worth doing for the reason you actually gave — not wanting to depend on reverse-engineered internals — rather than as a path back to the Store.

Net recommendation: **make this the new leading hypothesis for Q2** — public window-list cross-checking + self-tracking for detection, public keystroke simulation for switching, and accessibility-tree UI automation (not private symbols) only for the rare "create a new Space" case. Still needs the empirical spike either way, but now it's spiking a fully-public-framework approach first, with SkyLight/CGS as the fallback only if the accessibility tree turns out too thin to find the "+" reliably. Want me to write this into `architecture.md` and Q2 as the primary path?

- Refresh the mapping between currently open spaces and currently open projects, probably by checking whether windows we associate with those projects are in them.
- Figure out the current project by looking at which windows are currently visible, or saying “we aren’t in any obvious project now.”
- Select a space to use for a project — either the one currently assigned to it, or failing that one that’s currently not in use, or failing that create an entirely new one (and update the keyboard shortcuts and so on!)

### SpaceController (isolated Mac-only component)

Every Space-related operation Portal needs is factored behind one protocol, so the actual mechanism (public APIs vs. private frameworks) is an implementation detail that can change, be A/B tested, or be swapped without touching the dashboard, command grammar, or capture flow. Nothing above this component talks to `CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo`, `CGEventPost`, the Accessibility API, or SkyLight directly.

**Operations:**

- **`observeCurrentContext() -> ProjectID?`** — combines what would otherwise be two operations (refreshing the Space↔Project mapping, and figuring out the current project) into one, because both require the same underlying observation: which windows are visible right now. It checks currently on-screen windows (`CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo`, public) against the windows Portal knows it launched per project, infers the likely current project (or returns nothing if genuinely ambiguous — which safely degrades into the existing "no project context" capture behavior, not a new failure mode), and as a side effect updates the mapping entry for whichever Space this turns out to be. This is the same "one mechanism serving multiple purposes" shape already used for checkpoints — noticing it's current-project-detection *and* mapping-refresh at once, not two features to build separately.
- **`activateSpace(for: ProjectID)`** — switches to a project's Space: reuse the mapped Space if one exists, verified by content rather than trusted blindly (see self-healing note below); otherwise find a currently unassigned Space; otherwise create a new one and assign it. "Unassigned" can only be confirmed by actually visiting a Space and checking its windows (off-screen Spaces' contents aren't observable through public APIs), so this may need to cycle through Spaces the first time or after the cache goes stale — expected to be rare in steady state, since ordinary use continuously refreshes the mapping via `observeCurrentContext`.

**Self-healing address scheme.** Spaces are addressed by ordinal position (the same index the public "Switch to Desktop N" shortcuts use), stored in the local `SpaceMapping` (a local plist/SQLite file — unsynced machine state, per design decision 2 in `solution.md`). That index can drift if the user manually reorders Spaces outside Portal. Rather than trusting it blindly, every activation is verified against actual window content (`observeCurrentContext`'s check) — a mismatch means the mapping entry gets corrected on the spot rather than propagating a wrong guess. The index is a practical handle for switching; observed window content is the source of truth.

**Two swappable candidate implementations**, both satisfying the same protocol:

1. **Public-API hybrid (primary candidate):** `CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` for observation, `CGEventPost` synthesizing the public "Switch to Desktop N" shortcut for switching, and Accessibility-API UI automation of the Mission Control overview (the same public framework VoiceOver's Mission Control support relies on) to find and activate the "+" affordance for creating a new Space. No private frameworks; likely still incompatible with Mac App Store sandboxing rules around driving other processes via Accessibility, but that was never the deciding factor here.
2. **Private SkyLight/CGS symbols (fallback):** kept behind the same protocol in case the public-API hybrid's UI automation for Space creation, or its keyboard-shortcut-based switching, proves too unreliable in practice.

**Two implementation wrinkles surfaced during design, both rolled into the Q2 spike:**

- macOS doesn't enable "Switch to Desktop N" shortcuts for arbitrary N by default — as Space count grows, Portal may need to programmatically enable them (editing `com.apple.symbolichotkeys.plist`, a widely-used-by-utility-apps convention, not a blessed API but far more benign and reversible than `dlsym`-ing CGS symbols) or fall back to slower, visible Mission-Control-driven switching for Spaces beyond whatever's pre-enabled. Needs verification of current default behavior.
- Whether the Accessibility API actually exposes Mission Control's "+" affordance with enough structure to find and activate reliably is unverified — checkable directly with Xcode's Accessibility Inspector before committing.

# TODO

Concrete work items. Validation spikes here are *falsification tests* for load-bearing architectural bets — each one names what would make us change the design, not just "look into it." They are not the product test plan; that comes later.

## Validation spikes

### T1 — Can we switch to an arbitrary Space with public APIs? (Q2)

With 6+ Spaces configured, check System Settings → Keyboard → Shortcuts → Mission Control to see which "Switch to Desktop N" shortcuts are enabled by default. Confirm a `CGEventPost`-synthesized ctrl+N actually switches, and establish which TCC grant it needs (Accessibility, presumably) and how it degrades when that grant is revoked mid-session. If N > 4 is disabled by default, test writing `com.apple.symbolichotkeys.plist` plus `activateSettings -u` and check whether it takes effect without a logout.

**Passes if** Portal can switch to an arbitrary Space N in well under a second, without a logout. **If it fails**, fall back to Mission-Control-driven visible switching (slower, ugly) or to SkyLight/CGS.

### T2 — Is Mission Control's "+" reachable through the Accessibility API? (Q2)

Point Xcode's Accessibility Inspector at the Mission Control overview. Does the add-desktop affordance appear in the AX tree with a stable, identifiable role/label, and does `AXPress` on it actually create a Space? Check with multiple displays, and with "Displays have separate Spaces" both on and off, since those change the overview's structure.

**Passes if** we can create a new Space end to end through public frameworks. **If it fails**, Space creation moves to the SkyLight/CGS fallback implementation — contained behind `SpaceController`, so nothing above it changes.

### T3 — Can we observe windows without a Screen Recording grant? (Q2)

`CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` returns owner PID and bounds freely, but window *titles* require the Screen Recording grant on modern macOS. Portal's inference is supposed to key on the PIDs of processes it launched itself, which shouldn't need titles — verify that's actually sufficient. This matters more than it looks: needing Screen Recording would mean a scary, recurring permission prompt for a tool whose whole value is low friction.

**Passes if** current-project inference works with only the Accessibility grant, no Screen Recording.

### T4 — Does `gix` do a real three-way merge? (Q3)

Build two divergent branches and run three cases through `gix`: a cleanly auto-mergeable change, a genuine conflict, and a rename-plus-edit. The critical property is not that merges succeed — it's that the true conflict is *detected and surfaced*, never silently resolved. Confirm the resulting index/conflict state is usable enough to drive a real merge UI.

**Passes if** all three behave correctly, conflicts included. **If it fails**, switch to `git2`/libgit2 and accept the C cross-compilation cost.

### T5 — Does the Rust core actually cross-compile and bind? (Q3, and the core architectural bet)

The shared-core-plus-UniFFI decision is the single most load-bearing choice in the architecture, and it's cheap to falsify now and painful to discover later. Build the chosen git library plus UniFFI for `aarch64-apple-darwin` and `aarch64-linux-android`, call a function from both Swift and Kotlin, and do an authenticated HTTPS clone → commit → push against a private GitHub repo from each side. TLS is the likely sharp edge: `gix` uses `rustls` throughout, while `git2` means juggling a TLS backend per platform.

**Passes if** a full round trip works from both shells. **If it fails**, the whole shared-core strategy needs revisiting, not just the git library.

- Debounce tuning for idle-based auto-checkpoints — needs real usage data, not an upfront guess.

## Repository Layout and the Merge Surface

Git is the reconciliation engine for everything (design decision 7 in `solution.md`: explicit branches and disconnect branches go through one merge flow). Git's merge is line-based, which has a consequence worth stating plainly: **the conflict rate is a property of the file layout, not a fact of nature.** Two devices editing the same project while diverged is the normal case here, not an edge case, so layout is load-bearing architecture rather than a formatting detail. One principle covers most of it — make a file's line structure match its semantic unit of change, and never let position in a file carry meaning, because positional shifts are what turn independent edits into textual conflicts.

**Project registry: one file per project, not one registry file.** A single `registry.json` in the Home repo would be the most contended file in the system — every `/new`, every state change, from every device, all rewriting the same lines. Structured formats also merge especially badly: a botched three-way merge on JSON yields a syntactically *invalid* file rather than a marked-up one. Instead the registry is a directory of small per-project records (`registry/<project-id>.toml`). Two devices touching two different projects then produce disjoint changes that merge silently, and only concurrent edits to the *same* project conflict — which is rare, and genuinely a conflict when it happens.

**Lab notebook: one file per entry.** Appending is the highest-frequency operation in the system (every hotkey capture), and appending to the tail of a shared `notebook.md` conflicts *every single time* two diverged devices both do it — both add different lines at the same position. Entries therefore live as individual files, `notebook/<ISO-timestamp>-<device>.md`, a naming scheme where collision is impossible by construction and lexical order is chronological order. The notebook as a readable document becomes a rendered view rather than a stored file. *Trade-off worth naming explicitly:* this costs the ability to open one file and read the notebook straight through outside Portal — in a text editor, or on GitHub's web view. Portal could compile a read-only `notebook.md` on commit to buy that back; that reintroduces the contended file, but as a *regenerable artifact*, whose conflicts can always be resolved by rebuilding rather than by merging.

**TODO list and file/URL collection: one item per line, stable IDs, no meaningful order.** Unlike notebook entries, these items are *mutable* — checked off, reworded, deleted — and mutation is where merges get interesting. One item per line makes git's merge granularity match the item granularity, so checking something off on the phone while adding an item on the Mac merges cleanly. The critical rule is that **order within the file must never be meaningful**: sort order is a rendered property (a field on the item), because reordering on the Mac while checking one item off on the phone is a semantically trivial pair of edits that positional storage would inflate into a large textual conflict. Editing the same item on both devices stays a conflict, correctly.

**Unmergeable files need a declared policy — a real gap in "one merge flow."** Delegated files (design decision 10) are largely binary: an Illustrator file, a `.docx`, a PDF. Git cannot three-way merge them at all. The disconnect-branch flow can therefore produce a conflict that is not merely unresolved but *unresolvable on the device holding it* — a binary conflict surfaced on a phone that can't even open the file. The policy: Portal never blocks and never picks a winner. Both versions are kept, the incoming one renamed with its device and timestamp, and the collision is filed as a TODO item in the affected project. Nothing is lost, reconciliation never stalls, and the decision lands in front of the user on a machine where they can actually act on it.

**The fail-safe invariant for automatic merges.** Implicit reconciliation performs only *clean* merges. Any conflict at all — textual, or the binary case above — leaves the disconnect branch intact and unmerged and surfaces it on the dashboard as needing attention. Portal fast-forwards, merges cleanly, or stops and asks; it never auto-resolves. This is what the threat model's "auto-merge must fail safe" means concretely.

**Push contention is real even with a single user.** Two devices auto-checkpointing on idle will both try to push, and the loser gets a non-fast-forward rejection. The core's push path is therefore a fetch-merge-retry loop rather than a single push — and per the invariant above, if that merge isn't clean the push simply doesn't happen and the local branch waits. On Android this loop must survive being killed mid-flight, the same interruptibility requirement already noted for clone and fetch.

## Key Technology Decisions

It's the most load-bearing decision in the architecture and among the cheapest to falsify today.

**Then the architecture work — and the thread I pulled turned out to be the important one.**

Git is the reconciliation engine for everything, and git's merge is line-based. Which means: **the conflict rate is a property of our file layout, not a fact of nature.** Two devices diverged and both editing is the *normal* case here. That makes repo layout load-bearing architecture, not a formatting detail. The rule that falls out — make a file's line structure match its semantic unit of change, and never let position in a file carry meaning:

- **Registry**: one small file per project, not one `registry.json`. A single registry file would be the most-contended file in the system, and a botched three-way merge on JSON produces a *syntactically invalid* file rather than a marked-up one.

**One real gap surfaced.** "One merge flow" quietly assumed mergeable content — but delegated files are largely binary, and git can't three-way merge them at all. So a disconnect-branch can produce a conflict that's not just unresolved but *unresolvable on the device holding it*: a binary conflict on a phone that can't open the file. I've written a keep-both policy (retain both, rename the incoming one by device+timestamp, file a TODO) and added it to the threat model as a new medium-high risk. Never blocks, never picks a winner, never loses data.

I also made "auto-merge must fail safe" concrete: **automatic reconciliation performs only clean merges.** Any conflict leaves the branch intact and flags the dashboard. Fast-forward, merge cleanly, or stop and ask — never auto-resolve.

**One question genuinely needs your call**, since it's a values trade-off rather than a technical one: per-entry notebook files drive capture conflicts to zero, but you lose the ability to open one file and read the notebook straight through — in an editor, or on GitHub's web view. For a *lab notebook* specifically, that may matter more than it would for other data. My proposed compromise is having Portal regenerate a read-only `notebook.md` on commit: it reintroduces the contended file, but as a regenerable artifact whose conflicts are always resolvable by rebuilding rather than merging. Does that land right, or is straight-through readability important enough to want the primary storage to be one file?

## Repository Layout and the Merge Surface

Git is the reconciliation engine for everything (design decision 7 in `solution.md`: explicit branches and disconnect branches go through one merge flow). Git's merge is line-based, which has a consequence worth stating plainly: **the conflict rate is a property of the file layout, not a fact of nature.** Two devices editing the same project while diverged is the normal case here, not an edge case, so layout is load-bearing architecture rather than a formatting detail. One principle covers most of it — make a file's line structure match its semantic unit of change, and never let position in a file carry meaning, because positional shifts are what turn independent edits into textual conflicts.

**Project registry: one file per project, not one registry file.** A single `registry.json` in the Home repo would be the most contended file in the system — every `/new`, every state change, from every device, all rewriting the same lines. Structured formats also merge especially badly: a botched three-way merge on JSON yields a syntactically *invalid* file rather than a marked-up one. Instead the registry is a directory of small per-project records (`registry/<project-id>.toml`). Two devices touching two different projects then produce disjoint changes that merge silently, and only concurrent edits to the *same* project conflict — which is rare, and genuinely a conflict when it happens.

**Lab notebook: one file per entry.** Appending is the highest-frequency operation in the system (every hotkey capture), and appending to the tail of a shared `notebook.md` conflicts *every single time* two diverged devices both do it — both add different lines at the same position. Entries therefore live as individual files, `notebook/<ISO-timestamp>-<device>.md`, a naming scheme where collision is impossible by construction and lexical order is chronological order. The notebook as a readable document becomes a rendered view rather than a stored file. *Trade-off worth naming explicitly:* this costs the ability to open one file and read the notebook straight through outside Portal — in a text editor, or on GitHub's web view. Portal could compile a read-only `notebook.md` on commit to buy that back; that reintroduces the contended file, but as a *regenerable artifact*, whose conflicts can always be resolved by rebuilding rather than by merging.

**TODO list and file/URL collection: one item per line, stable IDs, no meaningful order.** Unlike notebook entries, these items are *mutable* — checked off, reworded, deleted — and mutation is where merges get interesting. One item per line makes git's merge granularity match the item granularity, so checking something off on the phone while adding an item on the Mac merges cleanly. The critical rule is that **order within the file must never be meaningful**: sort order is a rendered property (a field on the item), because reordering on the Mac while checking one item off on the phone is a semantically trivial pair of edits that positional storage would inflate into a large textual conflict. Editing the same item on both devices stays a conflict, correctly.

**Unmergeable files need a declared policy — a real gap in "one merge flow."** Delegated files (design decision 10) are largely binary: an Illustrator file, a `.docx`, a PDF. Git cannot three-way merge them at all. The disconnect-branch flow can therefore produce a conflict that is not merely unresolved but *unresolvable on the device holding it* — a binary conflict surfaced on a phone that can't open the file. Both versions are kept, the incoming one renamed with its device and timestamp, and the collision is filed as a TODO item in the affected project.
