# Integration: TODO

The reference implementation of the integration API — the only v1 type that exercises nearly all of it. Read alongside `software-architecture.md` §5; this document is both the TODO design and the worked example of what an integration *is*.

Source material: `02 file formats.md`. Decisions: D1 (structural merge), D3 (Portal owns no content types), D13 (parsing internal, typed domain ops), D20 (integrations do their own cross-project work), D26 (manifest and facet matrix).

## 1. What it owns

Everything about TODO lists: the file format, the structural merge, the per-project and cross-project views, and the "what am I doing today" flow. **Portal knows none of this** — not what "urgent" means, not what "today" means, not that hierarchy exists.

Facet matrix as it will appear in `integrations.toml`:

```toml
[todo]
roles      = ["todo"]
extensions = []                                          # identified by role, never by sniffing
core       = ["merge3", "diff", "domain"]
mac        = ["open", "presentDiff", "presentMerge", "widget"]
android    = ["open", "widget"]                           # merge UI deferred; conflicts defer to the Mac
```

## 2. File format

One item per line, indentation for hierarchy, inline tags. Taskpaper/todo.txt lineage: readable and editable in any text editor, and line-granular so git's merge granularity matches the item granularity.

```
- [ ] Finish the merge chapter @due(2026-09-01) !urgent ^k3f9
  - [>] Draft section 3 @today(2026-08-09) @touched(2026-08-09T11:04Z) ^m2p1
  - [x] Outline @touched(2026-08-07T14:22Z) ^q7r4
- [~] Talk to the [conference organizers](mailto:x@y.z) ^b8x2
- [-] Rewrite the intro ^v5n8
```

**Status markers** — five states, one glyph each: `[ ]` not started, `[>]` in progress, `[~]` paused, `[x]` done, `[-]` nevermind.

**Tags** — `@due(date)`, `@today(date)`, `@touched(timestamp)`, `!urgent`, `^id`. Links are ordinary markdown inline in the text, since they're part of what the item *says*.

**`@today` is self-expiring.** Storing the date rather than a boolean means an item marked for today simply stops matching tomorrow — no cleanup job, and its merge is a trivial union since marking something for today is additive and low-stakes.

**IDs are visible, and that's now acceptable.** They're the join key structural merge depends on (D1). Since the native UX is the common path and hand-editing the exception (D13), the cost of a visible `^k3f9` is low. *The sigil is a bikeshed to settle at implementation* — `^` is quiet and unlikely to collide, but `#id:` is unambiguous.

**Timestamps live in the file, unlike the notebook's.** The notebook derives ordering from commit timestamps (D1) because entries are append-only and map cleanly to commits. That doesn't work here: an item's status can change several times within one commit, and `git blame` is both expensive and fragile under re-indentation. So `@touched` is written by Portal whenever it changes a field. A hand-added item simply has none until Portal touches it, and merge degrades gracefully when it's absent (see §4).

## 3. Data model

```rust
struct TodoItem {
    id: ItemId,
    text: String,
    status: Status,             // NotStarted | InProgress | Paused | Done | Nevermind
    due: Option<Date>,
    urgent: bool,
    today: Option<Date>,
    touched: Option<Timestamp>,
    children: Vec<ItemId>,
}
```

Internal only — nothing outside the integration sees it (D13). Widgets go through the domain operations in §5.

**Archive is derived, not stored.** Done and nevermind items stay where they are and the view filters them out; making that a move into `todo-archive.md` would turn ticking a box — the single most common operation — into a two-file delete-plus-add, the worst case for merging. Compaction into a real archive file exists as a **deliberate, explicit** operation for when the list gets genuinely long, never automatic, because a move is merge-hostile and shouldn't happen behind your back.

## 4. `merge3`

Parse both sides into ID-keyed maps, then resolve per item.

| Case | Rule |
|---|---|
| In both, one side changed a field | Take the change |
| In both, both changed **different** fields | Merge field-wise — the payoff case: check it off on the phone while rewording on the Mac |
| In both, both changed **text** | Conflict region |
| In both, both changed **status** | Later `@touched` wins — *unless* both are terminal and differ (done vs nevermind), which is a real judgment call and becomes a conflict |
| In both, both **reparented** differently | Conflict, unless one side's new parent no longer exists, in which case take the other |
| In base + one side only | **Deleted by the other side.** Deletion loses to modification: if one side deleted and the other modified, keep the item and flag it |
| In one side only, not in base | Added — keep |
| **No ID** (hand-added) | Unmatchable. Treat each side's as an add: duplicates are visible and fixable, silent loss is not |
| Unparseable | Decline; the ladder falls to textual merge (rung 2) |

**Ordering is the subtle part, and it corrects an earlier claim.** The architecture previously said order "must never be meaningful." That's too strong: **order carries *user* meaning but not *system* meaning.** People arrange lists deliberately, and canonicalising on every write would rewrite arrangements behind their back. So the file preserves order, merge never *depends* on it, and merging two orders uses a deterministic list-merge (preserve ours, insert theirs' additions at their relative positions). Determinism comes from the algorithm, not from canonicalisation — which is what T6's "identical regardless of which side is ours" requires.

## 5. Domain operations

The API widgets use. Nothing here leaks the file format.

```rust
fn list(project: &ProjectId) -> Result<Vec<TodoItemView>>;
fn add(project: &ProjectId, text: &str, parent: Option<ItemId>) -> Result<ItemId>;
fn set_status(project: &ProjectId, id: ItemId, status: Status) -> Result<()>;
fn set_field(project: &ProjectId, id: ItemId, field: Field) -> Result<()>;   // due, urgent, today
fn reparent(project: &ProjectId, id: ItemId, parent: Option<ItemId>) -> Result<()>;
fn remove(project: &ProjectId, id: ItemId) -> Result<()>;

fn today_view() -> Result<TodayView>;                    // cross-project, §6
fn plan_session() -> Result<PlanningView>;               // the "what am I doing today" flow, §7
```

Every mutation is read-modify-write on the file through the git filesystem. The autosave loop handles committing; the integration never calls `sync` itself.

## 6. Cross-project: the unified view

The D20 proving case — the integration does this itself, over core primitives.

```
list_projects(Active)
  → for each: get_metadata(p).roles["todo"]      ← resolves where the TODO file lives
  → read(p, path)                                 ← clone if present, else GitHub blob
  → parse, filter, rank
```

**Surfacing policy** — entirely TODO's business, which is the whole point of D20. An item surfaces if it is `!urgent`, or `@due` within the horizon (or overdue), or `@today` matching today. Ranking: overdue, then urgent, then due-soon, then today-marked. Done and nevermind never surface.

Urgency changes with the clock rather than with edits, so the view recomputes on a timer, not only on change.

### What this exercise surfaced

**The integration surface needed one more primitive than we thought.** `list_projects` + `read` isn't sufficient: TODO must resolve *where* each project's list lives, which is `ProjectMetadata.roles`. So `get_metadata` belongs in the sanctioned integration surface too. Small, but exactly the kind of gap the proving case exists to find.

**Acting on another project's items is harder than reading them.** Ticking off an item from the unified view means writing to a project that may not be cloned — and `write` requires a clone (§2.10). Two ways out, and the second is better:

1. *Clone on demand when the user acts.* Correct, but cloning an entire repository to tick one checkbox is a poor trade on a phone.
2. *Remote write-through.* GitHub's contents API commits a single file change server-side, with the blob SHA as an optimistic-concurrency precondition — so it either applies cleanly or fails and you fall back to cloning. **This is a proposed addition to the git filesystem** and would make the phone genuinely useful across forty projects without holding forty clones. It needs assent before going into §2.10, since it adds a write path that bypasses local merge (safely, but it is a real change).

Without one of these, the unified view is read-only for uncloned projects — worth stating plainly rather than discovering in use.

## 7. The planning flow

The distinctive part of the app, and the reason it's worth writing rather than adopting something. `plan_session` presents pending items across active projects and lets you mark a set as today's work. Marking writes `@today(date)` and nothing else, so the commitment expires on its own.

Scope note: the *view* and the marking are v1; a richer flow (grouping by thread, estimating, deferring with a reason) is worth wanting but is not what makes v1 useful.

## 8. Widgets

- **Mac panel, project scope** — that project's list, hierarchical, with status toggles inline.
- **Mac panel, global scope** — today's items across projects, each labelled with its project.
- **Mac dashboard** — the full list plus the planning flow.
- **Android home-screen widget** — today's items, read-mostly, tapping opens the app.
- **Android screen** — per-project list and the global view.

Merge UI is Mac-only in v1 (see the facet matrix): a structural three-way merge needs more screen than a phone has, and conflicts defer to a capable device by design.

## 9. Open questions

- The ID sigil (`^k3f9` vs `#id:k3f9`) — settle at implementation.
- Compaction threshold and whether the archive keeps hierarchy or flattens to breadcrumbs.
- Whether `@created` is worth storing; nothing in v1 needs it, and it doubles per-item timestamp noise.
- Due-date horizon for surfacing (7 days is a guess and should meet real use).

Three good ones. The archival design in particular has a property worth naming.
All three in, as **D29**–**D31**.

**On lenient dates** — writing it up surfaced a bug I'd have shipped. **The default time has to be field-specific**: a bare `@due(2026-09-01)` means *end* of that day, and defaulting it to midnight makes everything due today instantly overdue. `@touched` defaults to start-of-day (past event, only needs rough ordering), and `@today` needs no time at all since it's a date match by definition.

It also forced a rule I'd been assuming without stating: **serialization must round-trip untouched lines byte-for-byte**. A read-modify-write rewrites the whole file, so without that, one edit normalizes every hand-typed date in the list and buries a small change in a large diff. Worth noting the churn is harmless for *merge* either way — structural merge compares parsed fields, so `2026-09-01` and `2026-09-01T23:59Z` are one value — but it's not harmless for a diff a human has to read. Generalized to all native formats as D31, since it applies equally to the notebook and FileSet.

**On archival — your design has a property worth naming explicitly.** Writing a **new dated file per run** (`todo-archive/YYMMDD.md`) makes archival **merge-free by construction**. It's the notebook's day-file trick applied again: two devices archiving produce different filenames and can never append-conflict, where a shared `todo-archive.md` would conflict every time two diverged devices archived. That's now in `notes.md` as a recurring move to reach for whenever a design wants multiple devices appending to one file.

The frozen-ancestor copy is the right call over the simpler alternative (an ancestor breadcrumb string), precisely because it keeps the IDs — which is what makes unarchiving reattach rather than guess. Reading the archive unions the files and dedupes by ID, preferring a real archived item over a frozen copy.

I added two conditions to make the awkward case nearly unreachable: archive only items **terminal beyond a threshold** (30 days, to tune) and only while the project is **Synced**. If a device archives something another concurrently modified, "deletion loses to modification" keeps it live with a stray archive copy — untidy, not lossy, self-correcting — but restricting to long-dead items in synced projects means it essentially never happens. That's a nice use of the state model: a race removed for free by checking a state we already compute.

**On `write_through`** — your framing is better than mine and I've adopted it. Calling it *the dual of `read`* is exactly right: `read` already resolves clone-or-remote, and this is the write side of that. Two things I'd add:

- **Explicit, never transparent.** Your "you'd only want this if you're doing something really explicit and cross-repo" is the design constraint. Making it something `write` resolves silently would invite it into code that should be doing an ordinary read-modify-write.
- **With a clone present, it routes locally.** Otherwise a server-side commit leaves you Behind your own working copy — an easy trap, avoided by having the explicit call still do the right thing in both cases.

Two honest caveats recorded: it's a *host* capability rather than a git one (would need reimplementing off GitHub), and the contents API caps files around 1 MB — fine for a TODO list, not for a manuscript.

Thirty-two decisions now. The queue's remaining substance: **notebook and FileSet** to this depth (both much smaller, and FileSet is load-bearing since the project manifest is one), the **`ProjectMetadata`/`FileSet` schemas**, and **T5** still being the cheapest thing that could invalidate a lot of this.
Which item is T5? I can’t remember which file lists those.

They're in **`Clarity Protocol/todo.md`**, as T1–T7.

**T5 — "Does the Rust core actually cross-compile and bind?"**

Build the chosen git library plus UniFFI for `aarch64-apple-darwin` and `aarch64-linux-android`, call a function from both Swift and Kotlin, and do an authenticated HTTPS clone → commit → push against a private GitHub repo from each side.

*Passes if* a full round trip works from both shells. *If it fails*, the whole shared-core strategy needs revisiting — not just the git library.

**Why it's the one I keep pointing at:** it tests the single most load-bearing decision in the architecture. Everything in `software-architecture.md` §2 — the git filesystem, the tick loop, `sync`, the merge ladder — assumes a Rust core with real Swift and Kotlin bindings on both platforms. If that assumption breaks, the fallback isn't "pick a different git library," it's reconsidering the shared-core approach entirely, which would invalidate a large fraction of what we've designed.

TLS is the likely sharp edge: `gix` uses `rustls` throughout, while `git2` means juggling a TLS backend per platform, and Android's NDK toolchain is where cross-compilation problems usually surface.

The full set, for reference:

| | |
|---|---|
| **T1** | Can we switch to an arbitrary Space with public APIs? |
| **T2** | Is Mission Control's "+" reachable through the Accessibility API? |
| **T3** | Can we observe windows without a Screen Recording grant? |
| **T4** | Does `gix` support the merge we actually need — including base/ours/theirs access for scratch-space merges? |
| **T5** | Does the Rust core cross-compile and bind, with authenticated HTTPS from both shells? |
| **T6** | Property-test the type-aware merge rules (not a spike — the highest-value correctness work) |
| **T7** | Does the panel keep capture at "gesture, type, enter"? |

T1–T3 all bear on Q2 (Space automation), T4–T5 on Q3 (git library). T6 and T7 aren't feasibility questions — T6 is correctness work listed there so it doesn't get treated as ordinary unit testing, and T7 is the condition that deferring the MessageBox rests on.

## D32: The git library is `git2`/libgit2, because `gitoxide` cannot push

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — resolves Q3. Evidence: `notes/03 T4 gix merge spike.md`, `notes/04 T5 cross-compilation and binding spike.md`.

**Decision.** The core's git filesystem is built on `git2` 0.21 / libgit2 1.9.6, with `vendored-libgit2` + `vendored-openssl` + `https` on Android and the system `Security.framework` on macOS.

**Why — and not for the reason Q3 expected.** Q3 framed this as a question about merge coverage, and on merge the two libraries are equal: T4 ran `gix` through clean auto-merge, genuine conflict detection, rename-plus-edit, the custom base/ours/theirs → own-resolution path, and binary conflict, and `gix` passed all of them, the custom path more cleanly than the test asked for. What decided it is that **`gitoxide` has no push implementation at all** — `gix-protocol` contains only `fetch`/`handshake`/`ls_refs`. `sync` is "commit everything outstanding, then try to push" (§2.4), so push is not a peripheral gap. Every T4 case was re-run against `git2`, which matched `gix` case for case and pushes.

The C cross-compilation cost this was expected to trade against turned out to be cheap: vendored libgit2 plus OpenSSL cross-compiled for `aarch64-linux-android` in 43 seconds.

**Consequences.**
- **The two platforms have genuinely different TLS stories**, as the platform note predicted: macOS links `Security.framework` and needs no OpenSSL; Android needs vendored OpenSSL, which ships **no trust anchors**, which is now a real and blocking implementation task (queued in `todo.md`). Android's `cacerts` use OpenSSL's legacy MD5 hash names, so no hashed-directory approach can ever work — settled, not worth re-testing.
- **I2 survives the library change for free.** `Repository::merge_trees` returns an *in-memory* `Index` and touches neither the working tree nor the on-disk index, so the scratch-space merge flow (§3) falls out of the library's natural shape rather than being defended against it.
- The three stages come from `index.conflicts()` (`ancestor`/`our`/`their`); custom resolution is `repo.blob()` → `conflict_remove()` → `add()` → `write_tree_to()` → `commit()`. Binary conflicts produce no stage-0 entry, so libgit2 never fabricates a merged binary and D16's rung-3 precondition holds.
- **The shared-core-plus-UniFFI bet is validated** as far as a spike can: one Rust crate, UniFFI 0.32 Swift and Kotlin bindings, an authenticated HTTPS clone → commit → push from Swift on macOS, and the same `.so` loading and executing on an arm64 Android emulator.
- `gix` stays worth watching. If it gains push it becomes a migration candidate, and `notes/03 T4 …` is already the specification of what the merge layer must do.

**The general lesson, which cost the most to learn.** `gix` is full of push-*shaped* symbols that are configuration rather than capability: `Direction::Push`, `push_url()`, `push_specs`, `Service::ReceivePack`. The API surface reads as though push exists. **Confirm a load-bearing capability by exercising it, not by finding vocabulary that names it.**

## D33: Append-union ordering needs a deterministic, side-independent tiebreak

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — amends D1 and the notebook rule in `architecture.md`. Evidence: `notes/03 T4 gix merge spike.md`, finding 3.

**Decision.** Where append-union orders two sides' blocks by commit time, equal timestamps are broken by comparing the two commit object ids as bytes.

**Why.** Git stores commit times at **second granularity**, and in testing two divergent commits landed in the same second on *every* run — this is what normally happens when two commits are made close together, not an edge case. The existing rule ("ordering comes from commit timestamps rather than in-file metadata") is therefore underspecified in the common case, and the tempting fix — break the tie by argument order — would violate T6's invariant that **a merge is identical regardless of which side is "ours."** Comparing object ids is stable, side-independent, and free.

**Consequences.**
- The rule belongs in the notebook format spec, not left to the implementation, since two devices must agree.
- The pre-existing judgment that clock skew can cosmetically mis-order two blocks within a day still stands and is untouched — this is about ties, not skew.
- T6 should generate same-second commits deliberately; they are common enough that a property test which never produces them is missing the ordinary case.

Let me check what's actually on disk versus memory first — one correction there.

**On the misremembering:** the only integration designed to depth is TODO (`solution/integration-todo.md`). Notebook and FileSet have *decisions* about them — append-union and the new ordering tiebreak (D1/D33), FileSet-as-Collection with directory targets and app overrides (D25) — but no integration document. They're still queued. Same for metadata: D24 settled that `ProjectMetadata` is a YAML file in the project and named the three confusable things apart (`ProjectMetadata` / `RegistryEntry` / `ProjectStatus`), but the actual schema is unwritten.

## The queue

**Bytes-on-disk decisions — cheap now, migrations later**
- Name the identifiers that end up in file paths and committed content: `ProjectId` (it's the filename in `registry/<project-id>.toml` — slug, UUID, or `owner/repo`?), `ItemId` (alphabet, length, collision behavior), `RoleId`/`TypeId` (open strings or closed enum — UniFFI will care).
- Native format specs: notebook, TODO, collection, registry records. Source material is `02 file formats.md`; now also has to carry D33's ordering tiebreak.
- Specify `ProjectMetadata` and `FileSet` — the YAML schema for roles, autosave mode, active FileSet, directory targets, app overrides.

**API-shaping decisions that want settling before the code exists**
- Design the machine-local store. Three unsynced things, only two named: the sync journal and the Space↔project map. The third — `ProjectId` → clone path — is undesigned, and it's the one whose loss *isn't* harmless: losing the journal degrades gracefully by construction (D21), losing the clone map orphans working copies holding unpushed work.
- Decide how a permanently deferred conflict gets unstuck. Rung 4 as a user-invocable escape, or automatic past a threshold. This shapes the merge API, so it's before-not-after.
- Write the integration interface and `integrations.toml`, then port notebook and TODO onto it as the proving cases.

**Then buildable**
- Headless dev CLI over the core, and T6 property testing.
- Design the notebook and FileSet integrations to `integration-todo.md`'s depth (needs the interface first).
- Android TLS trust — blocks all Android networking, but nothing before Android work.

**UI cluster, gated on one spike:** panel/widget-hosting contract, adoption UX, timeline/rewind, neglect signal. These are four items but really one substrate, and T7 hasn't run.

**Spikes still unrun:** T1–T3 (Space automation), T6, T7.

## What I'd do next

The identifiers. It's the smallest item in the queue and the only one that's *irreversible by default* — everything else can be redesigned on paper, but a `ProjectId` choice is in committed filenames on two devices the moment anything runs. It also blocks the format specs and the metadata schema, which in turn block the CLI having anything to read.

It should take one conversation, not a session. Then the format specs, which is the real work of that cluster.

Want to start there, or is something else pulling at you?

Sounds good, let’s discuss that. For project IDs, I think that using the git repo name (owner and repo) is the best choice because (a) these are guaranteed by github to be unique and (b) this produces great human readability and ease of switching between Portal and directly mucking about with git whenever needed. Any reason not to do this?

Three objections. Two are papercuts, one I think is decisive.

**The decisive one: not every project has an `owner/repo`.** D12 supports adopting a plain directory — `git init`, then scaffold — and D23's `AutosaveMode::LocalOnly` is a designed, supported configuration where a project never gets a remote at all. Those projects need a ProjectId from the moment they're registered, and there's nothing to derive one from. You'd need a second ID scheme for them, and then a migration when one later gains a remote — which is a rename of the identity, arriving through the exact path the next objection is about.

**The serious one: `owner/repo` is mutable, and this is a join key.** Repos get renamed as projects find their name; ownership transfers are rarer but real. GitHub redirects the URL, which is why this feels safe, but the identity underneath has changed. ProjectId isn't just the registry filename — it's the key into the clone-path map, the Space↔project map, and the sync journal, on two devices that have to agree. Rename on the Mac and the phone's registry still holds the old file: the merge sees a delete plus an add, which is the worst-shaped change in this system and the thing D30 went out of its way to avoid. Recoverable by hand, since it's all plain text and the project's actual content is untouched — annoying rather than catastrophic. But making it correct means a `renamed_from` field, a merge rule that recognizes the pair, and fixups across three machine-local stores. That's more machinery than the alternative costs.

Also worth noting on (a): GitHub's uniqueness guarantee is point-in-time, not historical. A freed name can be reused. Unlikely to bite one user, but it's a weaker guarantee than it looks.

**The papercuts:** GitHub is case-insensitive-preserving, macOS's filesystem is case-insensitive, and Android's is not — so `Zunger/Portal` and `zunger/portal` are one repo, one file, and two files respectively. Needs canonicalizing to lowercase or it's a real two-device bug. And the slash makes ProjectId a path *fragment* rather than a filename component, so anywhere it needs to be a single segment (an Android intent extra, a Space-map key) it needs escaping.

## What's right in the instinct, and where to put it

Point (b) is correct and worth preserving deliberately — but I'd separate where it applies. The place you actually muck about with git by hand is the *project clone*, and its path absolutely should be `owner/repo`. The Home repo's `registry/*.toml` is Portal's own bookkeeping; you read it to debug, not to work. So most of the ergonomic win survives an opaque ID, and it lands where you'd actually feel it.

This is also a tradeoff the architecture has already made once. D28: TODO items match by stable ID precisely so that the human-meaningful parts — order, text, hierarchy — stay free to change without breaking the join. Same shape here. A name that people read will get changed; a key that machines join on must not. One string can't be both, and the notes already flag "take a generalization only as far as it deletes concepts" — `owner/repo`-as-ID doesn't delete the rename problem, it just leaves it unhandled until it fires.

**Proposal:** ProjectId is a short opaque slug — lowercase alphanumeric, ~10 characters, generated at creation, never changes. `owner/repo` becomes a field on `RegistryEntry`, used for display everywhere and for the clone path. Renaming a repo then updates one field in one file, and nothing joins on it. As a bonus, ItemId is the next identifier on the list, so settling the alphabet and length once covers both.

**The alternative,** if you weight registry readability higher than I'm weighting it: a user-chosen slug at creation (`portal`, `ncii-paper`), decoupled from GitHub so there's less pressure to change it. You get readable registry filenames and stability — but uniqueness becomes the user's problem, and I'd expect the urge to rename it when a project's name changes, which walks back into the same trap with fewer guardrails.

Want me to write this up as a decision, or does the remoteless-project case suggest something different to you?

content:
Good question — let me enumerate from the actual API surface rather than from memory.
Enumerated from the source. It falls into three tiers, and the distribution is more lopsided than I expected.

## Tier 1 — durably written into git

1. **`registry/<project-id>.toml`** — the filename, in the Home repo.
2. **`RegistryEntry.id`** — one field inside that same file.

That's the complete list. Notably, **a project's own repo never contains its ProjectId**: `ProjectMetadata` holds `name`, `roles`, `autosave`, `active` and no identity field, by design — the project is self-describing but doesn't know what Portal calls it. And TODO links are "ordinary markdown inline in the text" (§ format), so no structured cross-project reference exists anywhere in content either.

## Tier 2 — machine-local, unsynced

3. The **clone-path map** (`ProjectId` → path) — still undesigned, queue item.
4. The **Space↔project map** (Mac only).
5. The **sync journal** — one record per project.

All rebuildable in principle; D21 already requires losing the journal to be harmless. The clone map is the one whose loss actually costs something.

## Tier 3 — API surface only, never persisted

~25 core functions take `&ProjectId` (`sync`, `read`, `write`, `write_through`, `status`, `timeline`, `rewind`, all six branch ops, `get_metadata`, `set_metadata`, `set_lifecycle`, …), four return one (`create_project`, `adopt_directory`, `adopt_repository`, `observeCurrentContext`), and the TODO integration's six domain ops carry it through. These cost nothing whatever the representation — it's a parameter type.

## What the enumeration changes

**I over-weighted the rename problem.** Since the ID is durably written in exactly one place, a rename under `owner/repo` is: one file renamed in the Home repo (a delete+add merge if two devices disagree) plus re-keying three local maps. Real, bounded, recoverable — not the scattered mess I implied. I'd downgrade that from "serious" to "a papercut with a sharp edge."

**But the remoteless case survives untouched, and it's worse than I put it.** `RegistryEntry` already declares `remote: Option<String>`. The written architecture *already says* a project may have no remote. Deriving identity from `owner/repo` doesn't just fail an edge case — it contradicts a field type that's already on the page. Either that `Option` is wrong, or `owner/repo` can't be the ID.

**And the cost of an opaque ID is now precisely measurable: one unreadable filename.** Not "the registry is unreadable" — the file's *contents* still carry `name` and `remote` in plain text, `list_projects` is what renders the dashboard, and finding a project by hand in a directory of small TOMLs is one grep. Meanwhile the clone path — the thing you actually `cd` into when mucking about with git — is free to be `owner/repo` regardless.

So the trade is: one opaque filename, against a scheme that contradicts an existing optional field and needs a rename protocol. I'd still take the opaque ID, but on much narrower grounds than I first argued — the readability loss is nearly nil, not that the rename cost is large.

One thing worth deciding alongside it: whether `RegistryEntry.id` should exist at all, given it duplicates the filename. Storing it makes the file self-contained if it's ever moved or copied; omitting it removes a way for the two to disagree. I'd lean toward keeping it and having the loader treat a mismatch as the filename winning.
Well, let me add a further twist: What information lives in `registry/<project-id>.toml`? And what would happen if instead we had a *single* registry.toml file?

## What's actually in it

Four fields. `id`, `name`, `remote: Option<String>`, `lifecycle`. About 150 bytes:

```toml
id = "…"
name = "Portal"
remote = "git@github.com:yonatanzunger/portal.git"
lifecycle = "active"
```

The split rule (§4) is "things true of the project everywhere travel with the project; things the dashboard needs to *list* projects live in the registry." So this file is deliberately tiny — it exists to render a dashboard without reading every project.

## What happens with a single `registry.toml`

The original rationale (architecture.md, "Project registry") was: it'd be the most contended file in the system, and *"structured formats merge especially badly, since a botched three-way merge on JSON yields a syntactically invalid file rather than a marked-up one."*

**That argument is now largely obsolete, and I think it was already obsolete before you asked.** It's an argument about *git's generic line merge*. Portal doesn't use git's generic merge on its own types — and D1 names the registry explicitly: "structural field-level merge for TODO items **and registry records**." The registry is already a declared native type with its own merge rule. Under structural merge keyed by project, two devices adding different projects produce two new records and union cleanly; two devices changing lifecycle on different projects touch disjoint records. That is the *same* conflict profile per-file layout gives you. One buys isolation from the filesystem, the other from an algorithm we've already committed to building.

The contention argument also doesn't survive scale-checking: a single user creates projects maybe monthly and changes lifecycle rarely. It's the most contended file in the registry, which is a near-zero baseline. The TODO file changes orders of magnitude more often and is happily one file per project.

**What one file buys, beyond that:**

- **ProjectId stops being a filename.** No slash-as-path-fragment problem. No case-sensitivity divergence between macOS and Android — it's a string compared by one parser under one rule, not by two filesystems under two.
- **Readability, better than readable filenames gave you.** `cat registry.toml` shows every project at once. That's the thing you actually wanted from `owner/repo`, and a directory of readable filenames is a worse version of it.
- **One blob fetch on mobile instead of N.** This one's underrated. The phone often has no clone of Home, so per-file means listing a directory via API then fetching N blobs — and that compounds with the cross-project view's existing per-project fan-out. One file is one fetch.

**What it costs — one real thing:** blast radius. A botched merge or a bad hand-edit takes out *every* project's record, not one. And lifecycle state is the one field in there that isn't derivable from anywhere else — you could rebuild `name` and `remote` by scanning GitHub and local clones, but active/back-burner/archived/pinned is genuine user data that exists nowhere else. Git history is the backstop, as always, so "lost" means "recover from history," not "gone." Still, it's a real downgrade: merge-free-*by-construction* traded for merge-correct-*by-algorithm*.

## The synthesis this suggests

Make it record-oriented and lenient, and the tradeoff mostly dissolves. If one project is one record with independent parsing — the same discipline D31 already sets for native formats, parse leniently and round-trip untouched records byte-for-byte — then an unparseable record loses one project and is preserved verbatim for the user to fix, rather than invalidating the file. Per-record blast radius, single-file readability.

And that reopens the identity question in a better place. With a single file you can have both halves of what you wanted:

- The **record key is the human name** — `owner/repo` when there is one, freely renameable, right there when you open the file.
- A **stable opaque `^id` inside the record** is what merge joins on and what the three machine-local maps key against.

That's D28 applied one level up: the name carries user meaning, the ID carries system meaning, and neither has to pretend to be the other. Renaming a repo becomes a one-line edit that merges as a field change. The remoteless project just has no `owner/repo` and shows under its `name`. The slash and case problems never arise because nothing is a filename.

Cost: one more field, and `list_projects` returns both. Compared to a rename protocol plus a second ID scheme for remoteless projects, that's cheap.

**One thing I'd resist,** flagging it because it'll be tempting when we write the format: making the registry an instance of Collection (D4). It looks like one — an ordered set of references with per-entry metadata. But D20's lesson says an abstraction covering two cases is only validated if it covers them *for the same reason*, and a Collection exists to be `open`ed while the registry exists to be indexed. Different consumer, different reason. Worth checking deliberately rather than assuming.

Shall I write this up — the single-file registry as an amendment to the per-file decision, plus the name/id split — or do you want to poke at the blast-radius question first?

Perfect and I agree — and this is definitely not the same as collection, this is a store for some very specific metadata. No reason for these to be the same. The blast radius question really doesn’t worry me, these failures are hopefully rare and given how easy it is to recover from git history, I’ll take the risk.

## D34: The registry is a single record-oriented file, not one file per project

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — reverses the per-project-file layout in `architecture.md`'s "Project registry."

**Decision.** The Home repo holds one `registry.toml`, one record per project, parsed per-record and leniently. It replaces `registry/<project-id>.toml`.

**Why the original rationale expired.** The per-file layout rested on two claims: that a single file would be the most contended in the system, and that "structured formats merge especially badly, since a botched three-way merge yields a syntactically *invalid* file." The second is an argument about **git's generic line merge** — and Portal doesn't use that on its own types. D1 already names registry records as taking structural field-level merge. Under structural merge keyed by project, two devices adding different projects union cleanly and two devices editing different projects touch disjoint records: the *same* conflict profile the per-file layout was bought for. One buys isolation from the filesystem, the other from an algorithm already committed to.

The contention claim doesn't survive scale-checking either. It's true only relative to a near-zero baseline — a single user creates projects rarely and changes lifecycle state rarely. A per-project TODO file changes orders of magnitude more often and is happily one file.

**What the single file buys.**
- **One blob fetch instead of N on mobile.** The phone often has no clone of Home, so per-file meant listing a directory over the API and then fetching N blobs — compounding with the cross-project view's existing per-project fan-out.
- **Readability, better than readable filenames would have given.** The whole picture is one `cat`.
- **ProjectId stops being a filename**, which removes the slash-as-path-fragment problem and, more seriously, a real two-device bug: macOS's filesystem is case-insensitive and Android's is not, so filename-keyed identity could diverge across devices. A key inside a file is compared by one parser under one rule.

**The cost, accepted.** Blast radius: a botched merge or bad hand-edit affects every record rather than one, and `lifecycle` is the one field derivable from nowhere else (`name` and `remote` could be rebuilt by scanning GitHub and local clones). Two things make this acceptable — per-record lenient parsing means an unparseable record loses one project and is preserved verbatim rather than invalidating the file (D31's discipline applied here), and git history makes any bad merge recoverable. Judged rare and cheap to recover from.

**Consequences.**
- The registry format must be **record-oriented**, not a monolithic structure where one syntax error is fatal. This is a constraint on the format spec, not a preference.
- What is lost in kind, and worth naming: merge-free-*by-construction* traded for merge-correct-*by-algorithm*. Acceptable only because the algorithm was already being built; it would not be if registry merge were new machinery.
- **Not a Collection (D4).** It looks like one — references with per-entry metadata — but D20's test asks whether two cases need an abstraction *for the same reason*, and a Collection exists to be `open`ed while the registry exists to be indexed. Different consumer, different reason.

## D35: `ProjectId` is a stable opaque id; the registry record's key is the human name

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — resolves the `ProjectId` half of `todo.md`'s identifier item. `ItemId`, `RoleId` and `TypeId` remain open.

**Decision.** `ProjectId` is a short opaque identifier — lowercase alphanumeric, generated at project creation, never changing. Each registry record is *keyed* by a human-facing name (`owner/repo` where one exists) which is freely renameable, and carries the stable id as a field. Merge joins on the id; every display and the clone path use the name.

**Why not `owner/repo` as the id, which was the starting proposal.** Two reasons survived examination, and one of them is decisive.

The decisive one: **not every project has an `owner/repo`.** D12 supports adopting a plain directory, and D23's `AutosaveMode::LocalOnly` is a supported configuration where a project never gets a remote. `RegistryEntry` already declares `remote: Option<String>` — so deriving identity from the remote doesn't merely fail an edge case, it contradicts a field type already in the design.

The second: **`owner/repo` is mutable.** Repos get renamed as projects find their name; ownership transfers happen. The id is the join key for the registry, the clone-path map, the Space↔project map, and the sync journal, on two devices that must agree — and a rename under a name-keyed identity presents to merge as a delete plus an add, the worst-shaped change in this system.

**Why the cost is small, which is what made this easy.** An enumeration of every occurrence found that `ProjectId` is durably written in exactly **one** place — the registry. A project's own repo never contains its id (`ProjectMetadata` holds name, roles, autosave, active, and no identity field), and no content format carries a structured cross-project reference: TODO links are ordinary markdown. Everywhere else it appears is either machine-local and rebuildable (three maps) or an API parameter type, where representation is free.

**Consequences.**
- **Renaming is a one-line field edit** that merges as an ordinary field change. No rename protocol, no `renamed_from`, no fixups.
- This is D28 one level up: the name carries *user* meaning and may change; the id carries *system* meaning and may not. Neither has to pretend to be the other.
- The name is not required to be unique or stable, so nothing needs to enforce it. It is a label.
- Alphabet and length should be settled together with `ItemId`, since both land in hand-editable files and there is no reason for two conventions.
- A record's key and its id can disagree if a file is hand-edited; the id wins, since it is what everything else joins on.

content:
Let me check two things in the TODO integration before answering — the archive filename scheme and what §9 already says about IDs.
The reasoning is right in shape, and the scoping instinct is the important part — but there's a missing term in the formula, and I think the model itself is the wrong one for this system.

## The missing term

`2·log2(n)` is the point where a collision becomes *likely*, not where it becomes unlikely. That's the birthday bound's expected-first-collision point, which sits at roughly 50%. Running your own numbers:

- 64k items in 32 bits: p ≈ (2¹⁶)²/(2·2³²) = **50%**
- 600 items in 20 bits: p ≈ 600²/(2·2²⁰) = 360,000/2,097,152 ≈ **17%**

So the month-scoped version isn't "highly unlikely," it's a coin flip every few months. The corrected form needs the target failure probability in it:

**bits ≈ 2·log₂(n) − 1 + log₂(1/p)**

For 600 items at one-in-a-million, that's 18.4 − 1 + 20 ≈ **38 bits**, not 20. The `log₂(1/p)` term is where all the safety lives, and dropping it is what makes 20 bits look sufficient.

(Worth noting: the example IDs already in `integration-todo.md` — `^k3f9`, `^m2p1` — are 4 base36 characters, almost exactly the 20 bits you derived. So the document currently encodes your estimate.)

## But the birthday model doesn't apply here

Birthday-bound reasoning assumes blind generation — you emit an ID with no ability to check. Portal is never in that position. It's writing an item into a file it has already parsed, so it can generate, check, and regenerate on collision. That reduces the *unavoidable* exposure to exactly one case: **items created independently on two devices during a divergence window**, where neither can see the other's IDs.

That n is small — call it 20 items per side in a realistic window. Expected collisions ≈ a·b/N:

- 20 bits: 400/2²⁰ ≈ **1 in 2,600** per divergence window
- 30 bits: 400/2³⁰ ≈ 1 in 2.7 million
- 40 bits: negligible

So under the model that actually governs, 30 bits would do.

## The failure mode is what should decide this

Here's the thing that pushes me toward generosity anyway. **A collision doesn't fail loudly — it fails silently, and it fails as data corruption.** Two genuinely different items sharing an ID don't look like a collision to structural merge; they look like *one item whose text and status disagree between the two sides*. Field-level merge will then do exactly what it's designed to do — take status from one side and text from the other — and produce a coherent-looking item that never existed, from two real items, one of which vanishes.

That is precisely the "silently corrupt content" risk the threat model ranks first, arriving through a side door. And the safety net doesn't catch it: git history preserves the pre-merge commits, but nobody will know to go looking, because nothing appeared to go wrong.

Given that, I'd choose the length that's safe under the **blind** model even though we'll implement the check — so that correctness doesn't depend on the check being right everywhere it's needed (hand-added items getting IDs assigned, archive files not loaded at generation time, a future integration reusing the scheme). Check-at-generation becomes defense in depth rather than load-bearing.

Per-project lifetime items, generously, ~20k. At 40 bits blind: 20,000²/(2·2⁴⁰) ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁴. At 30 bits: 0.18 — unacceptable. So **40 bits**.

**Concrete proposal:** Crockford base32 — digits plus consonants, excluding I, L, O, U. Exactly 5 bits per character, so 8 characters = 40 bits on the nose. The excluded letters are the ones that matter in a file people hand-edit: no 0/O or 1/l/I ambiguity when someone retypes an ID, and dropping U makes accidental profanity essentially impossible. Same alphabet and length for `ProjectId` — one convention, and 40 bits is vast overkill for a few hundred projects, but the id is a secondary field next to the human name (D35) so nothing is cramped by it.

The honest cost: `^k3f9q7m2` instead of `^k3f9`, four more characters on every line of a hand-editable file.

## Scope, which needs stating explicitly

`ItemId` must be unique across **one project's live TODO plus its entire archive** — not per-file, not global. That follows from D30: reading the archive unions its files and deduplicates by ID. Your instinct to bound it by the unarchive window is right about *why we keep the IDs*, but the dedup is what sets the uniqueness requirement, and it spans all archive files. Bounding it would mean scoping the dedup too, which costs more than the bits save.

## Other use cases — I found one, plus a category error

Sweeping the design: notebook day files use `YYMMDD-<words>.md` with no ID, and collisions there are benign by construction (two files for one date, both render). TODO archive files are `todo-archive/YYMMDD.md`, and same-day archival on two devices produces the same filename with *identical content*, because archival is deterministic given its two conditions — no disambiguator needed. Merge scratch is keyed by git's own commit oids. FileSet entries have no IDs and presumably join on target path, which is worth confirming when FileSet gets designed rather than assuming.

The one genuinely unnamed identifier: the sync journal carries a `device: String` field (§2.9). It's machine-local with n=2, so entropy is a non-question, but it's undesigned — worth folding into the machine-local store item.

**And `RoleId`/`TypeId` are a different kind of question entirely.** They're vocabulary — `notebook`, `todo`, `fileset` — not generated identifiers. Nothing about collision probability applies; the actual question is open strings versus a closed enum, which is about extensibility and what UniFFI can express. I'd keep it out of this decision so it doesn't get answered by analogy.

Want me to record this as a decision, or does the 8-character cost in the TODO file feel too steep for what it buys?

Nope, feels exactly right — I was working on a calculator as you were thinking and coming to pretty much the same place. 8 Crockford characters it is. 

And yes, RoleId and TypeId are completely a separate question; let’s write this one up and then move on to that one.

## D36: Generated identifiers are 8 Crockford base32 characters

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — settles `ItemId` and the concrete form of `ProjectId` (D35). `RoleId`/`TypeId` are a separate question and deliberately not covered.

**Decision.** Every generated identifier — `ItemId`, `ProjectId` — is 8 characters of Crockford base32 (digits plus consonants, excluding `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), giving exactly 40 bits. One convention for both. Portal checks for collision at generation time and regenerates on a hit.

**Why 40 bits, when far fewer would do.** Two models give very different answers, and we sized against the pessimistic one deliberately.

Under the model that actually governs, the requirement is tiny. Portal never generates blind — it is writing into a file it has already parsed, so it can check. The only unavoidable exposure is items created independently **on two devices during a divergence window**, where neither can see the other's ids. At ~20 items per side, 30 bits already gives one collision in 2.7 million windows.

Under blind generation — no check — the requirement is a project's whole item history, ~20k items, where 30 bits fails badly (p ≈ 0.18) and 40 bits is comfortable (p ≈ 2×10⁻⁴). **We sized for blind generation so that the check is defense in depth rather than load-bearing.** The check has to be right in several places that are easy to miss: assigning ids to hand-added items, generating while archive files aren't loaded, and any future integration reusing the scheme.

**What made generosity worth paying for: the failure is silent, and it is data corruption.** Two different items sharing an id do not present to structural merge as a collision. They present as *one* item whose text and status disagree between sides — so field-level merge does exactly what it is designed to do, takes status from one side and text from the other, and produces a coherent-looking item that never existed, from two real items, one of which disappears. That is the threat model's top-ranked risk (unsafe auto-merge corrupting content) reached through a side door, and the usual backstop doesn't help: git history preserves both pre-merge commits, but nobody goes looking, because nothing appeared to go wrong.

**Why Crockford specifically.** Exactly 5 bits per character, so 8 characters is 40 bits with no waste. More importantly the excluded letters are the ones that matter in a file people hand-edit: no `0`/`O` or `1`/`l`/`I` ambiguity when someone retypes an id, and dropping `U` makes accidental profanity essentially impossible.

**Consequences.**
- The visible cost is real and accepted: `^k3f9q7m2` rather than `^k3f9`, four extra characters on every line of a hand-editable file.
- **`ItemId` uniqueness is scoped to one project's live TODO plus its entire archive**, because D30 deduplicates by id across the union of archive files. Not per-file, not global. Bounding it to a recent window would mean scoping the dedup too, which costs more than the bits save.
- Collision-check-and-regenerate is a **requirement on every id-generating path**, not an optimization.
- `ProjectId` is wildly over-provisioned at 40 bits for a few hundred projects. Accepted: one convention deletes a concept, and the id sits beside a human-facing name (D35), so nothing is cramped by it.
- The `^` vs `#id:` sigil remains an open bikeshed; 8 characters doesn't change that argument.

**A note on the method, which generalizes.** The first pass sized these with `bits ≈ 2·log₂(n)` — the birthday bound's expected-first-collision point, which is ~50% probability, not a safety margin. The corrected form is `bits ≈ 2·log₂(n) − 1 + log₂(1/p)`; the `log₂(1/p)` term is where all the safety lives. But the more useful correction was noticing that the birthday model **assumes blind generation** and Portal is never blind, which reframed the question entirely — from "how many items will exist" to "how many can be created without seeing each other."

content:
Pulled the definitions from the source.

## The distinction

**`TypeId` selects an integration** — the code that knows how to handle a kind of content. It's a global namespace, one entry per integration, declared in `integrations.toml`. The v1 roster (D27) is exactly five: `todo`, `notebook`, `fileset`, `text`, `binary`. It answers *"what code handles this file?"*

**`RoleId` names a slot inside a project** — a purpose that some path fills. It's declared per-project in `ProjectMetadata.roles`, mapping role → path: `notebook -> "notebook/"`, `todo -> "todo.md"`. It answers *"what is this path **for** in this project?"*

They connect at type resolution (§1.2), whose first and highest-priority rule is: a path under a declared role takes that role's type. That's how the notebook and TODO list get identified *by where they are* rather than by sniffing their contents — which is what lets an adopted repo keep its own layout (D12) instead of having Portal's imposed on it.

## Why they look redundant, and where they aren't

In v1 the mapping is nearly the identity function: role `todo` → type `todo`, role `notebook` → type `notebook`. That's why they're confusable.

The case that justifies two concepts is D4's collections. A project can hold *several* FileSets — the `active` manifest that `open` launches, and, say, a research project's `bibliography` — and D4 is explicit that these are "distinguished by the role each is declared under rather than by being distinct types." So: **one type, many roles.** Roles are also where user extension lives — adoption "chooses where roles live," and a bibliography is a role a user invents, not one Portal ships.

That asymmetry mostly answers the question on its own: `TypeId` is closed by construction (it's the set of integrations we shipped, enumerable at build time, and D26's checkable facet matrix *requires* it be enumerable), while `RoleId` wants to be open.

## Two gaps this surfaces

**1. Open roles can't currently resolve to a type.** `TypeClaim` declares `roles: Vec<RoleId>` — "roles this type serves" — as a static list in `integrations.toml`. But an integration can't statically claim a role name a user invents. So if someone declares `bibliography -> refs.toml`, resolution step 1 finds no claiming type, falls through to extension/UTI, and a `.toml` bibliography lands on **generic text**. Wrong answer, silently.

Either roles are effectively closed to what integrations claim — contradicting D4 — or `ProjectMetadata.roles` has to carry the type alongside the path, something like `bibliography -> (refs.toml, fileset)`. The second is more consistent with D24's principle that a project is self-describing, and it would let `TypeClaim.roles` shrink to a scaffolding default or disappear entirely — one fewer mechanism.

**2. The registry needs a merge rule but isn't in the type roster.** D1 says structural field-level merge covers "TODO items *and registry records*," but D27's five integrations don't include a registry type. D34 sharpened this: the registry is now a single structurally-merged file, and the merge ladder dispatches by type. So either it's a sixth integration, or the core special-cases its own bookkeeping outside the integration surface — defensible, since it isn't user content, but it needs saying rather than being an omission. Home's "one reserved role" is presumably this, and it's never been named.

Neither gap is hard, but both change what the `RoleId`/`TypeId` decision has to say. Want to take them in order — settle the open/closed question first and let it dictate the schema, or work out the resolution path for user-declared roles first and see what it implies?

Indeed, as I’m thinking about the difference, TypeId is basically a generalized concept of file types, but RoleId is quite a fuzzy thing; I’m noticing that in the examples you’re giving, nearly all of these roles are really “how a particular app uses its particular data within projects.” The fact that the TODO app’s files live in a top-level whatever.todo file (for example) is really part of the TODO app’s design, not Portal’s! The only roles that are truly native to Portal are the files that it itself uses for things like the registry — e.g., the “active files” FileSet that `open` is ultimately going to surface in the Mac UI.

That's the D3 test applied to a namespace rather than to code — "who owns this vocabulary?" turning out to be the same question as "who owns this behavior?" And I think it's right, with a sharper consequence than you may have intended.

**Check the two Portal-native roles you named — neither actually uses the role mechanism.**

The `active` FileSet is already an inline field on `ProjectMetadata` (`active: FileSet`, D25), not a role→path binding. And the registry, post-D34, is a fixed `registry.toml` at a known location in a reserved repo — it doesn't need a per-project path declaration because Home isn't a varying case. Home's "one reserved role," mentioned once in `architecture.md` and never named, looks like it may be machinery that was never needed.

So if the integration-owned roles move to their integrations, and Portal's own two turn out not to be roles at all, then **`RoleId` as a Portal-level namespace dissolves entirely.** What replaces it is narrower and more honest: *Portal stores a per-project binding on behalf of each integration, and doesn't know what any of them mean.* Portal is the registrar, not the owner. It knows that in this project, whatever `todo` is, it lives at `todo.md`.

**That kills the first gap outright.** The reason user-declared roles couldn't resolve to a type was that `TypeClaim.roles` is a static list an integration can't extend with names a user invents. Once the binding is keyed *by* type, resolution is a lookup with the answer already in the key — no `TypeClaim.roles` at all. Two concepts deleted rather than added, which is the test from `notes.md` for whether a generalization is earning its keep.

**What survives, and it's the interesting residual:** you still need a discriminator when one type has several bindings — D4's project holding both an `active` manifest and a `bibliography`, both FileSets. But that label is now scoped *under* the type rather than living in a global namespace, so `fileset:bibliography` can't collide with anything and carries its own resolution. The thing that was doing real work in `RoleId` was never the name; it was the type association, and that's now structural.

**The second gap is orthogonal and doesn't move.** The registry still needs a merge rule (D1 promises structural field-level merge for registry records) while not being in D27's five-integration roster. Restructuring roles doesn't answer whether the registry is a sixth integration or core-internal bookkeeping outside the integration surface. D34 made that more pressing, not less.

**One risk worth naming before we commit.** "Portal stores per-integration binding data it doesn't understand" is one short step from "Portal stores arbitrary per-integration config," which is the generic record store the architecture explicitly refused to build ("no manifest DSL and no generic record store"). The discipline that keeps it honest is keeping the binding to *paths only* — where your data lives, nothing else. If an integration wants settings, those belong in its own file in the project, where they merge under its own rules and cost Portal nothing.

The open question this leaves is what the binding's shape is: `Map<TypeId, Path>` is too thin for the notebook (a directory) plus TODO (a file plus an archive directory) plus multi-instance FileSets. Want to work that out, or first settle whether the registry is an integration — since if it is, it's a sixth binding and wants to fit the same shape?

So I can take us even further than that: Why does Portal need to store a per-project binding at all? Portal itself really only cares about the files inside a project in very limited ways — it needs to know what to call for the facet operations like open and merge. If it knows that there’s a `.todo` file type and that the registered TODO integration handles it, that’s all it cares about.

One thing that becomes interesting in this case is that some of the logical “files” we want are actually directories. FileSet is a good example, because it would contain both a central registry that’s the actual list of things in the fileset — presumably its own custom format that we build using YAML or whatever — and a bunch of actual files in formats like .pdf and so on. Of course, in this case the merge logic is that of the individual files as per their own formats, plus a custom logic for the registry file itself, so really the only “custom file type” is that registry type.

A better example might be Mac applications, which are directories whose name ends in .app. Here we can identify its “app nature” from the directory name, and if we want to be properly careful by validating its directory structure, but an important principle is that it’s easy to recurse a larger directory structure containing one and immediately tag “this directory is an app, and so should be handled by the app handler rather than recursing into it.”

All of which is to say: Maybe all we need is a concept of filetypes and the associated ways to handle them for facet operations?

content:
That's a real simplification, and I think it works — but it needs one addition to cover the notebook. Let me check the source material first.
Checked `02 file formats.md` — and it confirms the case that forces one addition. The notebook is inherently a folder, and its day files are `.md`. Under pure extension typing they'd resolve to generic text and silently lose append-union merge.

So the rule you need is the one your FileSet example already implies, generalized: **containment in a typed bundle is itself a type-resolution rule.** A `whatever.notebook/` directory declares that `.md` files directly inside it are day files. That's precisely what the role rule was doing — "a path under a declared role takes that role's type" — except the declaration now travels with the directory name instead of living in per-project state. Same power, no metadata.

With that, yes: file types and their handlers are all you need.

## Two flavors of bundle, and the distinction does work

Your `.app` point is sharper than tidiness. It's the difference between:

- **Opaque bundles** (`.app`) — tag it, don't recurse, hand the whole directory to the handler. Merge is display-and-pick or keep-both at directory granularity. Essentially generic binary, one scale up.
- **Transparent bundles** (`.notebook`, `.fileset`) — recurse, but the bundle types its own contents. Its manifest gets a custom type; everything else merges by its own type, exactly as you described for FileSet's PDFs.

That's a real bit in the design and it should be declared, not inferred. Note it also answers "what does merge mean on a directory," which the merge ladder currently has no story for.

## What this deletes

`RoleId`, `TypeClaim.roles`, per-project bindings, and the "choose where roles live" step in the adoption flow. Plus a good signal: `resolve_type(project, path)` stops needing project metadata and becomes context-free — it only needs the path's own ancestry.

**And it resolves the registry gap for free.** The registry just becomes a file type. Check it against the facets: structural `merge3` ✓ (which is what D1 promised and D34 now depends on), domain operations ✓ (`list_projects`, `set_lifecycle`), and a widget — the dashboard's project picker. That's a complete integration, and it clears D27's bar easily, since generic text merge on the registry is exactly the outcome D34 needs to avoid. The roster goes to six, and Home's mysterious "one reserved role" disappears entirely.

## The honest costs

**Cross-project TODO lookup changes shape.** Today it's `get_metadata(p).roles["todo"]`. Now it's "find the `.todo` files," which forces a question roles had answered by fiat: what if there are three? Plausibly "all of them" — arguably better, since a project might legitimately want several lists — but it's a decision, not a detail. And `get_metadata`'s original justification evaporates; `integration-todo.md` records that it was added to the sanctioned surface *specifically* to resolve role→path.

**`ProjectMetadata` shrinks to almost nothing** — name and autosave mode, since the `active` FileSet could itself just be a `.fileset` in the project, found by name. Worth asking whether it still earns being a file.

**Renaming a file changes its type.** `todo.todo` → `todo.txt` silently becomes generic text and loses structural merge; under roles the binding survived renames. It's how every OS works and the loss is visible (the widget stops rendering it), so I'd accept it — but it's a genuine regression in robustness, and it's the one thing roles were better at.

**Adoption gets simpler rather than harder**, which is worth saying because it looks like a loss. An adopted repo keeps its layout automatically. And the flexibility roles seemed to offer was partly illusory: pointing Portal at an existing `TODO.md` still required that file to be in Portal's format, so it was never "adopt the todo list you already have."

**Downstream:** this changes the format specs materially — `todo.md` and `notebook/` become `something.todo` and `something.notebook/`. That's the queue item that was about to become transcription, so better to hit it now.

The thing I'd want to settle before writing this up is the bundle declaration itself: how a type declares that it's a bundle, opaque or transparent, and how it types its contents. Nested bundles need a rule too (outermost wins, presumably). Shall we work that out?

Looking at the costs, I think the TODO one resolves by moving all of that logic into the TODO app. It would be quite reasonable for that app to say “your top-level todo file is always in <repo>/.todo” or the like and solve the problem that way. It’s an app design problem, not a platform one.

Renaming changing the type is nothing new at all, this is highly expected behavior in basically every OS in the world nowadays.

What I think we need to lock down is a way to write a type declaration, which I think is part of the integration’s manifest — one or more type declarations, essentially. These should include a name for the type (we’ll assign a unique ID when we load it in to avoid collision), a way to check if a URL is of the type (may be false for types that never present as such), and a way to check if a path in the repo is of the type — which can also return whether or not one should be allowed to recurse into it. Since type identification is done depth-first that would solve the nesting question.

That resolves both cleanly — and the TODO one is the better answer, since "where my file lives" being app design rather than platform design is the same D3 boundary we've been drawing all along.

On the declaration shape: I agree with it, with one structural amendment and two smaller pushbacks.

## First, note what just happened to D13

D13 explicitly moved *away* from per-integration `claims` predicates to central resolution, and its stated reason was that "the notebook and TODO list are identified by *where they are* rather than by sniffing their contents, so a chain of per-integration predicates was the wrong shape." That premise was the role mechanism. We just deleted it — so the rationale expired, exactly as the registry-layout rationale did. Second time in one session; the `notes.md` entry about re-checking premises is earning its keep.

But D13 had *other* concerns worth preserving, and they argue for a hybrid rather than a straight return to predicates.

## The amendment: declaration is data, the predicate is a veto

A pure predicate chain loses three things:

- **Conflict detection.** If two integrations both claim `*.todo`, a predicate chain silently resolves by order. As data, it's a load-time error — which is what it actually is.
- **Cost.** Depth-first over a repo × N integrations is N predicate calls per path, each possibly touching content. Suffix matching is a hash lookup.
- **Checkability (D26).** The manifest's whole value is being statically inspectable. Code isn't.

So: **match declaratively, validate procedurally.** The declaration carries path patterns; the optional predicate can only *reject* a match, never claim one. That's exactly your `.app` case — identify by name, then optionally validate the directory structure — and it keeps everything above.

```toml
[notebook]
paths    = ["*.notebook"]
bundle   = "transparent"
contents = { "*.md" = "notebook" }        # what replaces the role rule
core     = ["merge3", "diff", "domain"]
mac      = ["open", "presentMerge", "widget"]

[app]
paths    = ["*.app"]
bundle   = "opaque"                        # tag it, don't recurse
validate = true                            # optional structure check, may reject
```

The `contents` table is the piece that has to be explicit, because it's what carries the notebook's day-file typing — the one thing roles were genuinely doing. It also stays declarative, where "`.md` directly inside a `.notebook`" as a predicate would not be checkable.

I'd also lean toward `bundle` being a static property rather than something the path check returns per-call, for the same checkability reason — unless you can think of a type that's sometimes opaque and sometimes not.

Your depth-first point holds and gives the right nesting semantics: pre-order traversal, check the directory before descending, **outermost wins**. A `.app` inside a `.fileset` stops at the app. Nested transparent bundles compose naturally.

## Two pushbacks

**The assigned unique ID may be solving the wrong problem.** If two integrations declare the same type name, that's a configuration bug — assigning them distinct IDs papers over it silently. Names must be unique in the manifest, which D26's checkable manifest already enforces, so the name *is* the unique identifier and a collision should be a load-time error. And nothing persists a TypeId: types are re-resolved from paths on whatever device is looking, so there's no cross-device or cross-run stability requirement that a numeric handle would satisfy. With a roster of six, I'd skip the indirection unless you see a use I'm missing.

**URL typing has no v1 consumer.** The only place URLs appear is `FileSetEntry::Url`, and URLs never merge — they're content Portal doesn't store — so URL typing feeds only shell-side `open` dispatch. Both platforms already route by scheme, and D3 says capabilities are a runtime query to the OS rather than a table we maintain. So it'd be a hook nothing calls. I'd leave the shape open for it and not build it, unless you're picturing a Portal-aware integration claiming particular URL patterns.

Want me to write this up? It's a large change — it retires `RoleId`, amends D13, D24 and D27, adds the registry as a sixth type, and rewrites the type-resolution section — so it'd be one decision with a fair number of consequences, plus edits across `architecture.md`, `software-architecture.md`, and `integration-todo.md`.
I like this a lot. I think you’re right about the assigned unique ID, let’s drop it — and let’s drop URL’s for now too, as per your point. Let’s make the change and adopt this.

input.new_string:
## D37: Roles are retired; a file's type comes from its own name, and directories can be typed

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — supersedes the type-resolution half of D13, retires `RoleId` entirely, and amends D4, D12, D24 and D26.

**Decision.** There is one concept, **file type**, and no per-project binding of any kind. A type is declared in `integrations.toml` with: a unique name, one or more **path patterns** it matches, whether it is a **bundle** and if so whether opaque or transparent, and for transparent bundles a **contents table** typing the files inside it. An optional validation predicate may *reject* a match but can never claim one. Resolution walks the tree depth-first, pre-order, checking each directory before descending; **outermost wins**, and an opaque bundle is never recursed into.

```toml
[notebook]
paths    = ["*.notebook"]
bundle   = "transparent"
contents = { "*.md" = "notebook" }        # what replaces the role rule
core     = ["merge3", "diff", "domain"]
mac      = ["open", "presentMerge", "widget"]

[app]
paths    = ["*.app"]
bundle   = "opaque"                        # tag it, don't recurse
validate = true                            # structure check; may reject, never claims
```

**Why roles had to go: they were the wrong owner.** Nearly every role was really *"how a particular integration lays out its own data."* That the TODO list lives at a given path is the TODO integration's design, not Portal's — the same D3 boundary the whole architecture is drawn along, applied to a namespace instead of to code. And when the genuinely Portal-native roles were checked, neither needed the mechanism: the `active` FileSet is already an inline metadata field (D25), and the registry is a fixed path in a reserved repo (D34). Home's "one reserved role," mentioned once in `architecture.md` and never named, was machinery that was never needed.

**Why bundles are required, not a convenience.** The notebook is inherently a folder of `.md` day files (`02 file formats.md`). By extension alone those resolve to generic text and silently lose append-union merge — so a directory must be able to type its own contents. That is exactly what the role rule did ("a path under a declared role takes that role's type"), except the declaration now travels with the directory name rather than living in per-project state. The two flavours matter: **transparent** bundles recurse and type their contents (notebook, FileSet — where ordinary PDFs inside still merge by their own type, and only the manifest is custom); **opaque** bundles are handed whole to a handler and never recursed into (`.app`), which is also what finally gives merge a defined meaning at directory granularity.

**Why matching is declarative and validation procedural.** D13 moved away from per-integration `claims` predicates for reasons that were only *partly* about roles, and those reasons survive: a predicate chain resolves two competing claims silently by order, costs N calls per path, and can't be statically inspected — which would gut D26's checkable manifest. So patterns are data (conflicts are a load-time error, matching is a hash lookup, the matrix stays inspectable) and the predicate is a veto that refines a match already made. `.app` is the motivating case: identify by name, then optionally validate the directory structure.

**Consequences.**
- **`RoleId` ceases to exist.** So does `TypeClaim.roles`, the "choose where roles live" step in adoption, and `ProjectMetadata.roles`.
- `resolve_type` **becomes context-free** — it needs the path's ancestry, not the project's metadata. Losing a parameter is the signal this was the right cut.
- **`ProjectMetadata` shrinks to name and autosave mode**, since `active` can itself be a `.fileset` found by name. Whether it still earns being a file is now an open question rather than a settled one.
- **The type name is the identity.** No runtime-assigned id: nothing persists a `TypeId` (types are re-resolved from paths on whichever device is looking), the roster is deliberately tiny, and two integrations declaring one name is a configuration bug that should fail at load rather than being silently disambiguated.
- **URL typing is not built in v1.** URLs appear only as `FileSetEntry::Url`, never merge, and both platforms already route by scheme — which D3 already says is a runtime OS query rather than a table we keep. The shape stays open; nothing calls it yet.
- **Portal's native formats need real extensions**: `something.todo`, `something.notebook/`. This changes the format specs, which were about to be transcription.
- **Renaming a file changes its type**, where a role binding survived a rename. Accepted: it is how every OS behaves, and the loss is visible (the widget stops rendering it) rather than silent.
- **Adoption gets simpler, not harder.** An adopted repo keeps its layout automatically. The flexibility roles appeared to offer was partly illusory anyway — pointing Portal at an existing `TODO.md` still required that file to be in Portal's format, so it was never "adopt the list you already have."
- Cross-project lookups stop going through `get_metadata`, which removes the *original* justification for adding it to the sanctioned surface. Where an integration's data lives inside a project is now that integration's own design problem.

## D38: The registry is a file type, and the v1 roster is six

**Date:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** decided — amends D27 (five types) and closes a gap D34 had sharpened.

**Decision.** The project registry is a declared file type with its own integration, bringing the v1 roster to six: TODO, notebook, FileSet, registry, generic text, generic binary.

**Why.** D1 promised structural field-level merge for "TODO items *and registry records*," but no registry type existed in D27's roster to provide it — and D34 made that load-bearing by consolidating the registry into a single structurally-merged file, since falling through to generic text merge is precisely the outcome it must avoid. Once types are resolved from names (D37), the fix is free: the registry is simply a file whose type is `registry`.

It also clears D27's bar comfortably, which is the test for whether a new integration is justified rather than merely distinct. It has a real `merge3` (field-level, keyed by `ProjectId`), real domain operations (`list_projects`, `set_lifecycle`), and a real widget — the dashboard's project picker, which is consistent with D5's "the panel and the full dashboard are the same widget set at two presentations."

**Consequences.**
- The dashboard becomes a widget over the registry type rather than bespoke Portal UI, which is the same move that made the notebook and TODO list widgets.
- Home stops being structurally special. It is a project containing a registry file, which is what "Home is a Project, not a separate kind of thing" always claimed.
- D27's rule is unchanged and still binding: the roster grew because generic behaviour was *wrong* here, not because the registry is a distinct kind of file.
